item.title: Christianity Today, a Voice of Centrist Evangelicalism, Is in Turmoil
item.description:
Last year, leaders of the evangelical publication Christianity Today summoned the entire staff to a hotel ballroom in the Chicago suburbs for a meeting about their future.

The publication’s chief operating officer, Nicole Massie Martin, opened her presentation with a Bible verse from the Old Testament about rejoicing even in dark times, “though the olive crop fails and the fields produce no food.” Then Thomas Addington, the interim president, delivered a blunt message: Christianity Today’s reputation as a staid voice of intellectual centrist evangelicalism — embodied by its proximity to Wheaton College in Illinois — had to change.

Christianity Today needed to be less like Wheaton and more like TikTok, Mr. Addington told his staff, according to several people who attended the meeting. Warning that layoffs were coming, he ended his presentation with a prayer. A senior editor left the room in tears.

Fourteen months later, more than half of the 79 employees at that time have either been laid off or resigned, including an editor in chief and four of the company’s longest-tenured journalists.

In interviews, a number of employees who have departed since the meeting in 2025 said that the changes at Christianity Today seemed to be about more than stabilizing its finances. Its new leaders, they believe, are abandoning the publication’s longtime commitment to independent journalism, a record that includes investigating accounts of misconduct by high-profile evangelicals.

Bonnie Kristian, Christianity Today’s deputy editor until last week, described its new leaders as being driven “by fear, by the kind of anxiety about reputational and financial loss that makes bold, interesting, principled journalism very difficult.”

Multiple journalists said that Ms. Martin and Mr. Addington have made attempts to discourage certain articles and lines of reporting based on feedback from their own social and professional circles. One reporter, who was granted anonymity because of concerns over the terms of his severance agreement, said he was instructed this year to slow down an investigation into a faith-based organization that had financial connections to Christianity Today.

“Every journalistic organization has debates about what content to prioritize,” Mr. Addington said. “C.T. is no different.” At the meeting in 2025, he said, he was using Wheaton and TikTok as “metaphors for where C.T. has been and where the media environment is taking us.” The outlet remains committed to independent journalism, he said.

Last week, the magazine’s new editor in chief, Erik Petrik, took down an article that discussed evidence that the popular evangelical writer Elisabeth Elliot, who died in 2015, was bisexual. Edited and fact-checked over the course of weeks, the article disappeared within 12 hours of publication, after receiving backlash from conservatives online.

The next day, the article reappeared with a note from Mr. Petrik saying that it “was not reviewed prior to publication by some key members of our content team.”

Mr. Petrik declined to say whether he would have published the article if it had been proposed under his watch. As the outlet’s top editor, “I will be cautious when facts are few and controversy high,” he said.

Christianity Today was founded in 1956 by a group of evangelicals including Billy Graham, and quickly became the flagship magazine of American evangelicalism.

Of the many Christian publications that flowered after World War II, it was the only one that insisted on “thorough reporting and professional reporters doing that work from the start,” said Daniel Silliman, who broke a major story for the magazine about accusations of sexual abuse against the high-profile evangelist Ravi Zacharias in 2020.

Mr. Silliman was later asked to investigate accusations of harassment against the magazine’s former editor in chief, the uncomfortable results of which the outlet published without having to seek review by its previous executives.

Along with reporting, Christianity Today publishes spiritual reflections, theological treatises and opinion essays that have long served as a bellwether for mainstream American evangelical sentiments. For decades, it generally avoided partisan battles and was read by Christian leaders and churchgoers across the country.

The Trump years upended the landscape of Christian journalism, and revealed gaps between publishers and the pews. Marvin Olasky, the longtime editor of the evangelical World magazine, resigned in 2021 as the magazine shifted from hard-hitting reporting to opinion journalism of the generally pro-Trump variety. The Christian Post, another evangelical outlet, also shifted to embrace President Trump.

Its 2019, Christianity Today made waves when it called in an editorial for the removal of Mr. Trump. It continued reporting both favorably and critically on the impact of the administration’s policies on refugees, foreign aid, gender policy and child care subsidies, to name a few. Russell Moore, a prominent evangelical critic of Mr. Trump, served as its editor in chief from 2022 to 2025.

The new Christian right that embraced Mr. Trump derides the magazine as “woke” and irrelevant.

The magazine’s woes are not straightforwardly partisan. In one case, Ms. Martin, who wrote in Christianity Today that she voted for Kamala Harris in 2024, proposed publishing a response by a group of Latino evangelicals who objected to an editorial by a Trump supporter.

But its issues reflect wider dilemmas within evangelicalism a decade into the Trump era, when many traditional conservatives still feel politically homeless.

“Can you have a centrist evangelical magazine?” asked Kara Bettis Carvalho, a former senior editor who left for The Boston Globe in May. The magazine’s leaders, she said, have “struggled to figure out our audience.”

Christianity Today has also been buffeted by the ordinary vagaries of the 21st-century publishing industry. The outlet has just over 50,000 paid subscribers in print and digitally, down from 80,000 magazine subscribers a decade ago. It increasingly relies on grants and fund-raising to pay the bills.

Ms. Martin, whose academic and professional background is in Christian ministry, was named president and chief executive at the end of last year. Mr. Addington, a former board member who founded an Arkansas-based e-commerce and logistics company, became its chief operating officer. Both immediately became involved with editorial decision-making to a degree that rattled many editors and reporters.

Christianity Today has a code of ethics that emphasizes its independence. “We maintain strict separation (the news industry term is a firewall) between editorial decisions and sources of all revenue,” it reads.

Ms. Kristian, the magazine’s former deputy editor, said Ms. Martin and Mr. Addington had discouraged or tried to dramatically revise multiple articles, apparently under pressure by the articles’ subjects or others unhappy with their impact.

Ms. Martin said she does not have formal oversight over content, but has asked to be notified before publication when something “may cause contention or affect our external brand in any way.” She said she has not intervened in editorial decision-making, but has simply asked questions about planned articles and passed along feedback from outside the company.

The future of Christianity Today is as a “journalism ministry that helps people make sense of the world through a biblical lens,” she said.

“Nicole has repeatedly affirmed C.T.’s journalism and C.T.’s editorial independence even though she’s violating it,” Ms. Kristian said. “In the meantime, Tom has been openly hostile.”

In a meeting in July, according to notes Ms. Kristian took at the time, Mr. Addington said that “editorial independence and autonomy are taken way too far,” and complained that he had no input into what writers were working on.

Mr. Silliman was suspended last fall by the magazine’s editor in chief at the time, Mr. Olasky, formerly of World, over a news article about a lawsuit against a California megachurch and its high-profile pastor, Greg Laurie.

It soon became clear to the reporter that it was Mr. Addington who had initiated the punishment. Mr. Addington told Mr. Silliman and his editor, Kate Shellnutt, that he was going to fly to California to personally apologize to Mr. Laurie for the article, which he described as unfair. (Mr. Addington said he and Ms. Martin offered to meet with Mr. Laurie, but schedules prevented the meeting from taking place.)

At one point, Mr. Silliman recalled, Mr. Addington wondered out loud why so many of his friends said Christianity Today was “feminine” and “woke.”

Mr. Silliman and Ms. Shellnutt quit the magazine in protest in late 2025. Ms. Kristian resigned in September. Mr. Olasky moved up his planned retirement from the end of the year to last week, after a new wave of layoffs in September left him with half his original editorial staff.

“The end of this era for us also represents something bigger about the evangelical movement,” Ms. Shellnutt said. “It’s a real narrowing of where hard stories can be told and where good stories can be told alongside them.”

In a recent virtual meeting with the staff, Mr. Petrik, the company’s sixth editor in chief in less than seven years, laid out his vision for Christianity Today’s next chapter. The outlet would be smaller, he said, but would maintain its high standards.

And, he added, “we’re going to be gentle in our tone.”

item.title: Calling Putin a ‘Humanitarian,’ Witkoff Thanks Him for Releasing an American
item.description:
Praising President Vladimir V. Putin as a “humanitarian,” the Trump administration envoy Steve Witkoff on Wednesday thanked the Russian leader in St. Petersburg for releasing an American man held for over four years on what the State Department called fabricated charges.

The release came after President Trump made a direct appeal to Mr. Putin to let the 74-year-old teacher, Stephen James Hubbard, return to the United States. Russia had accused Mr. Hubbard of being a Ukrainian mercenary.

“You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian,” Mr. Witkoff told Mr. Putin. “You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that.”

The Russian leader, who started a war of aggression against Ukraine that has led to the deaths of tens of thousands of Ukrainian soldiers and civilians, is wanted as a war criminal by the International Criminal Court.

Mr. Witkoff’s remarks came at the start of talks in St. Petersburg, where Mr. Witkoff had come to discuss new variants of a proposed plan to end the war that began with Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Mr. Hubbard was released unilaterally by Russia, rather than in a prisoner swap, at a moment when Mr. Putin has scored a succession of victories in winning Mr. Trump over to Russia’s side in the conflict.

In the past two weeks, Mr. Trump has announced that the United States will buy Russian diesel fuel and suspend the imposition of sanctions under the Lindsey Graham Act, named for the pro-Ukrainian senator who died this year. Mr. Trump also called on Ukraine to replace President Volodymyr Zelensky, Mr. Putin’s nemesis.

Turning over Mr. Hubbard, who was tortured, sometimes starved and placed in the general prison population in a country where he did not speak the language, came at little cost to Mr. Putin. But the move buys him good will with Mr. Trump, who is arguing that he alone has the relationship with Mr. Putin needed to get him to end the war.

Mr. Trump telegraphed that he had sought Mr. Hubbard’s release, talking to reporters about it on Tuesday, when the former teacher was still in captivity. But Mr. Trump didn’t mention that Mr. Hubbard was being held because Mr. Putin’s government had sought to take American prisoners for leverage.

In recent days, as he was moved out of a penal colony and prepared for release, it became clear that Mr. Hubbard’s value to Mr. Putin had changed. He was now more valuable to the Russian leader as a symbol of the renewed relationship with the U.S. president than as a pawn in negotiations.

Mr. Hubbard’s health is fragile. The Trump administration has pushed for his release since learning of his case, making it a priority, lawyers for Mr. Hubbard said. He will be flown to a State Department facility in Texas for evaluation and treatment.

The decision by Mr. Putin to release Mr. Hubbard came after a tumultuous 12 days in which Mr. Trump has repeatedly sided with Russia and sidelined Ukraine.

Ukraine said the United States had intermittently cut off intelligence sharing; limited its access to Starshield, the military version of the satellite internet service Starlink; and suspended delivery of its already limited supply of Patriot interceptors, the only defense Ukraine has against Russian ballistic missiles.

Mr. Hubbard was essentially abducted by Russian soldiers from eastern Ukraine shortly after Russia invaded and accused of fighting for Ukraine. Russian sentencing documents said he was given the call signs, or nicknames, of “Samurai” and “Ninja,” and that he manned a checkpoint on a bridge over a river.

This was highly unlikely.

Mr. Hubbard, a Michigan native, was living in the city of Izium, near Kharkiv, after a peripatetic life, teaching English for years in Japan and moving for a time to Cyprus, where one of his sons lived, before settling down with a Ukrainian woman. After that relationship ended, Mr. Hubbard opted to stay in Ukraine.

He had just turned 70 when the Russians invaded. His son in Japan told him to keep his head down, but Mr. Hubbard did not seem to understand that the war had started, text messages between the two men showed. Those messages also showed no evidence that Mr. Hubbard had joined the Ukrainian military. He told his son that all was well. He gave daily updates, like when he went to church. He had a hard time buying food, but said once that he bought caviar “for nutrition.”

The Russians said they arrested him inside the home of an acquaintance in April 2022.

Ukrainian prisoners of war who were held with Mr. Hubbard later told The New York Times that he had been repeatedly tortured because he was an American — beaten, forced to stand all day, given little food and poor medical care. In interviews after they were released, the Ukrainians said they feared for Mr. Hubbard’s life.

In October 2024, a Russian court convicted Mr. Hubbard of being a mercenary and sentenced him to almost seven years in a penal colony.

Unlike other Americans held in the Russian prison system, Mr. Hubbard was kept in the general population, his lawyers said. At times, his family had no idea where he was and the U.S. embassy had no access to him.

Mr. Hubbard was designated by the State Department as wrongfully detained in January 2025.

Shortly afterward, Martin De Luca, a former federal prosecutor instrumental in winning the release in February 2025 of another American held by Russia, started working on Mr. Hubbard’s case.

EPAM Law, a Moscow law firm that worked with Mr. De Luca on that earlier release, found out that Mr. Hubbard was being held in the IK-12 penal colony in Mordovia, the southwestern Russian region commonly referred to as “prison land.” In May 2025, Mr. Hubbard was allowed to call his son in Cyprus, Joseph Coleman.

Mr. Coleman, who is a Greek Orthodox priest, wrote a long letter to Mr. Putin in September, making a point of his Orthodox faith, similar to Russian Orthodox, and pleading for his father’s release.

“It’s amazing that he’s been released and we’re grateful to President Trump,” Mr. De Luca said. “I would characterize this as a small dividend on the hard road to peace.”

item.title: Toledo Residents Ordered to Evacuate After Chemical Explosion
item.description:
Nearly 1,000 residents in Toledo, Ohio, have been ordered to evacuate after an explosion at a chemical trucking company on Tuesday led to a leak of hazardous material, city and company officials said.

One person was injured at the scene, Mayor Wade Kapszukiewicz of Toledo said in a news conference on Wednesday morning.

The chemical released was glycidyl methacrylate, which is “used to make certain plastics, paints and coatings perform better,” according to a written statement about the incident from MC Transport.

Residents within a one-mile radius of the company’s terminal have been ordered to evacuate. The order initially consisted of a half-mile radius and was expanded overnight. The mayor noted that the area affected was more industrial than residential.

Early on Wednesday morning, Toledo Fire and Rescue also urged people within a three-mile radius of the site to shelter in place, to keep pets inside, close all windows and doors, and turn off any ventilation that might bring outside air inside.

The chemical, when emitted into the air, is a gas, the mayor said, but eventually will return to a liquid state. Emergency response teams have not yet been able to assess the explosion site, he said.

“There’s still concern that the tank is emitting this chemical and it has the potential within 12 hours of the incident to be explosive,” Mr. Kapszukiewicz said, adding that a hazardous materials team would reassess this morning.

The mayor said a foggy morning had made some residents more anxious, as they awoke to a hazy scene outside their windows, causing “a concern that the plume is extending larger than it really is.”

This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

item.title: Supreme Court Blocks Trump From Denying Gender-Transition Care to Federal Prisoners
item.description:
The Supreme Court on Wednesday prevented the Trump administration from immediately denying certain gender-transition medical treatments for transgender inmates at federal prisons.

The court’s unsigned, unexplained order was a rare example of the conservative-dominated bench siding, at least temporarily, with the rights of transgender individuals. Two conservative justices, Samuel A. Alito Jr. and Clarence Thomas, said they would have granted the administration’s emergency request to stop the treatments.

Under President Trump, the Bureau of Prisons adopted new policies that would prohibit inmates from receiving the care. Three transgender people in federal custody initially challenged the new rules. All three had previously been diagnosed with gender dysphoria by prison medical officials and had been prescribed treatments.

The ruling means that, for now, as many as 1,000 federal prisoners who have been diagnosed with gender dysphoria will continue to receive gender transition treatments that the Trump administration has attempted to restrict.

The lawsuit argued that the administration’s change in policy violated Eighth Amendment protections against cruel and unusual punishment. The policy has been blocked since June 2025, and the court’s ruling means that block remains in place while litigation about the issue proceeds.

Li Nowlin-Sohl, a lawyer with the American Civil Liberties Union’s LGBTQ & HIV Project, called Wednesday’s order a “critical ruling.”

“The attempted denial of medically necessary health care, including gender-affirming health care, to people in prison is a violation of their fundamental constitutional rights,” she said in a statement.

Audrey Cook, the Justice Department’s press secretary, said that while the court’s order is disappointing, it is not the final word on the administration’s policy.

“We look forward to pursuing our appeal in the D.C. Circuit to reinstate BOP’s policy that affirms biological reality,” she said in a statement.

In January 2025, President Trump issued an executive order barring prison officials from spending federal funds on “any medical procedure, treatment, or drug” to address gender dysphoria — a medical condition defined as the significant distress linked to a mismatch between a person’s birth sex and gender identity.

Earlier this year, prison officials issued a policy to implement Mr. Trump’s executive order. The policy permitted other forms of care for people with gender dysphoria, including psychotherapy and medications such as antidepressants.

The prison policy is one of a series of actions by the administration targeting transgender people. The president also directed government agencies to withdraw federal funding from schools that allow transgender athletes to participate in girls’ and women’s sports, and the administration has sought to bar transgender people from the military.

The ban has also been challenged in court, and the administration has asked the Supreme Court to allow the U.S. military to fully enforce it. The case is pending.

At the Supreme Court, the justices in June upheld state laws barring transgender female athletes from playing on girls’ and women’s teams. Last year, the justices also upheld a state law prohibiting some medical treatments for transgender youths, rejecting arguments that the law violated the Constitution.

In a narrower case from Idaho in 2020, the court similarly turned down a request from state prison officials to block court-ordered sex reassignment surgery for a transgender prisoner. Justices Alito and Thomas also said in that case that they would have granted the prison officials’ request.

In Wednesday’s case involving federal prisoners, Judge Royce C. Lamberth of the District Court in Washington, has issued a series of rulings ordering prison officials to continue providing medical care to the inmates. Those treatments have included hormone therapy, surgery and social accommodations such as makeup and wigs.

In June, Judge Lamberth found that “no adverse impacts on public safety or the operation of the criminal justice system” would result from maintaining the status quo while litigation continued.

“Denying individuals with gender dysphoria the ability to socially transition or obtain hormone therapy will predictably lead to mental health risks,” he wrote. “These risks include exacerbated depression, anxiety, suicidal ideation and self-harm.”

D. John Sauer, the solicitor general, asked the justices to intervene on an emergency basis, arguing that the rulings blocking policy were thwarting a step that prison administrators had “determined is necessary to maintain institutional security.”

In defending its new policy, the Bureau of Prisons said that the benefits to inmates of providing such care “no longer outweighed BOP’s other security and prison-administration concerns.”

If allowed to proceed, the government’s plan would mean that inmates who had been receiving treatment would be required to taper off their use of the medication, in a “rapid discontinuation of the hormone intervention.” Social accommodations such as makeup would be confiscated.

Lawyers for the transgender prisoners told the justices in court filings that gender-transition treatment is the only approach known to effectively treat gender dysphoria and that prison officials have provided hormone therapy to transgender inmates dating back to at least 1992.

Prison officials are seeking to “cut off treatment that its health care providers had recommended for decades,” according to lawyers from the American Civil Liberties Union. In addition, the lawyers said, prison officials have “not pointed to a single security incident relating to its provision of this treatment over the past 30 years.”

item.title: In Trump’s World of International Diplomacy, Insults Are a One-Way Street
item.description:
The rules of the road when it comes to President Trump’s relations with foreign leaders are clear: He may trash you. But woe unto you if you whack back.

No one knows that better than President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine, who has been through this particular diplomatic wringer more than once. But he got a pointed reminder during a closed-door meeting in Oslo this week with Mr. Trump’s negotiators.

Steve Witkoff, the president’s special envoy, and Jared Kushner, the president’s son-in-law, reproached Mr. Zelensky on Tuesday for his sharp comments responding to Mr. Trump’s sharp comments about him, telling the Ukrainian leader that the way he had conducted himself had infuriated the president, according to a person informed about the exchange.

Mr. Zelensky pushed back at times during the discussion as the Americans complained about certain remarks. “I never said that,” Mr. Zelensky insisted at one point, according to the person, who shared details on the condition of anonymity because it was a private conversation. But he clearly got the message. When he addressed journalists afterward, a subdued Mr. Zelensky strained to offer a positive assessment while sidestepping his recent criticisms of Mr. Trump.

“We are thankful to the American side,” Mr. Zelensky said, citing the resumption of U.S. intelligence help. He noted that he had spoken with Secretary of State Marco Rubio on his way to Oslo, which produced “positive signals from the American side” and that he had a “very constructive dialogue” with Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner. “But,” he added, “it was very constructive between us because all of us want peace: Ukraine, Europe, United States.”

The one-way-street school of diplomacy has worked for Mr. Trump in the sense that his belligerence leaves many world leaders reluctant to cross him for fear of blowback or even, depending on his mood, a fresh round of tariffs. Mr. Trump demands deference while rarely giving any, except to those who accede to his wishes or to those he courts, notably autocrats like President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia, President Xi Jinping of China and Kim Jong-un of North Korea.

The contrast between Mr. Trump’s attitude toward autocrats versus democrats was made all the sharper a day after the Oslo meeting, when Mr. Witkoff landed in St. Petersburg for peace talks. Upon securing the release of an American held prisoner in Russia, Mr. Witkoff called Mr. Putin, who faces an international arrest warrant for war crimes, “a humanitarian.”

Mr. Zelensky has been one of the exceptions in openly challenging Mr. Trump at times. But he has to calibrate how far he can push that because his country remains dependent on the United States for its survival as it defends itself against Russia’s invasion.

The Oslo meeting was intended to smooth over the latest rift. Mr. Witkoff stopped in the Norwegian capital before heading to St. Petersburg. Mr. Kushner, who was ill, did not accompany Mr. Witkoff, but joined the conversation via video link.

Mr. Trump’s recent shift further toward Moscow has prompted much speculation that it may be related to the upcoming midterm elections. But Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner went on at length during their conversation with Mr. Zelensky to deny any connection to domestic politics, according to the person informed about the session.

Mr. Zelensky had two friends with him for the encounter: his host, Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store of Norway, and the visiting President Alexander Stubb of Finland. Both of them have been strong backers of Ukraine and like most European leaders do not share Mr. Trump’s tilt toward Russia, but at the same time labor not to rile him unnecessarily.

“I’m happy that we were able to get together today to straighten out a few things and to agree that what matters now is to look ahead,” Mr. Store said. “There’s nothing to gain from digging into what was said yesterday or a week ago. We now really have to be focused on what lies ahead.”

Mr. Stubb expressed hope that the back-and-forth with Washington would now end. “Today was a success and tomorrow is a new day and hopefully we don’t do any backtracking,” he said.

Mr. Store and Mr. Stubb organized the meeting in Oslo in hopes of getting peace negotiations back on track. The notion that Mr. Witkoff would have gone to Russia to meet with Mr. Putin without seeing Mr. Zelensky first would have resulted in terrible optics, two European officials said. The meeting in Oslo would not fully resolve the fundamental issues, they added, but there is no real alternative to American leadership.

The White House did not immediately comment on the Oslo meeting. An American close to the talks said that the participants had a frank but respectful exchange that allowed them “to clear the air” and move forward. Mr. Zelensky’s public criticism of Mr. Trump may serve his own short-term political objectives, the American warned, but is ultimately counterproductive to Ukraine’s longer-term goals of ending the war.

This has been the calculation that many world leaders have had to make, particularly in Mr. Trump’s second term — when to respond in kind when the American president lashes out and when to swallow pride in the interest of not poking the bear.

For years, presidents and prime ministers of allied nations went out of their way to avoid angering Mr. Trump, who prefers escalation over conciliation. But in recent months, especially since his threats to take over Greenland last winter, leaders have shown less submissiveness and more willingness to stand firm.

Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada has led the way with his defiance of Mr. Trump’s attempts to strong-arm America’s northern neighbor into making trade concessions. Rather than back down, as leaders often did in Mr. Trump’s first term, Mr. Carney decided “to hit back” and slapped on dollar-for-dollar tariffs in retaliation.

Mr. Zelensky’s situation, however, is more complicated. Mr. Trump has been predisposed against Ukraine since his first term, convinced by advisers that Kyiv meddled in the 2016 election against him, an unfounded assertion that intelligence agencies have called Russian disinformation. His effort in 2019 to pressure Mr. Zelensky into opening an investigation into his Democratic rival, Joseph R. Biden Jr., led to Mr. Trump’s first impeachment for abuse of power.

The tone for the second term was set shortly after Mr. Trump returned to power last year and berated Mr. Zelensky in an explosive Oval Office meeting. Mr. Zelensky demonstrated at the time that he was unafraid to stand up to the president. But under coaching from European leaders and congressional allies, Mr. Zelensky has since mostly sought to avoid direct confrontations.

The past two weeks made that more difficult as Mr. Trump, who has long had a convivial relationship with Mr. Putin, pivoted even more dramatically in Moscow’s direction. Among other things, Mr. Trump and his team have struck a deal to buy Russian diesel fuel, lifted some sanctions and exempted Russia from others included in legislation that he just signed, curbed some intelligence and satellite assistance for Kyiv, delayed the delivery of interceptors and worked to broker an agreement to sell lucrative Russian oil assets to people with ties to Mr. Trump’s circle.

Mr. Trump has lashed out repeatedly against Mr. Zelensky in recent days, calling it “disgraceful” for Ukraine to strike Russian oil refineries and insisting that it “damn well stop.” He once again blamed Mr. Zelensky for the war that Mr. Putin started and said that “Russia has been fine” even as intensifying Russian missile and drone barrages are killing more civilians in Ukraine than at any time since the beginning of the full-scale invasion.

Mr. Trump went so far as to demand that Ukraine “get a new president” instead of Mr. Zelensky. By contrast, he has had no tough words for Mr. Putin, saying that he did not want to “do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table.”

It goes well beyond diplomatic protocol to explicitly push for the ouster of the leader of a fellow democracy. But when Mr. Zelensky responded by calling the diesel move a “weak decision,” suggesting that he felt “betrayed” and indicating that it seemed that Washington was trying “to convince Ukraine to capitulate,” Mr. Trump adopted the role of the aggrieved party.

Just hours before the Oslo meeting, he again lay the responsibility for making peace on Ukraine rather than Mr. Putin, who could end the war tomorrow by stopping his attacks on his neighbor. “Zelensky has to want to settle this war,” Mr. Trump told reporters in Washington. “And if he doesn’t, I think it’s going to be a very bad thing.”

Mr. Trump’s assertion that Mr. Zelensky, rather than Mr. Putin, is the obstacle to peace offends Ukrainians and Europeans alike. Mr. Zelensky emphasized in Oslo that, after all, his people are the ones under bombardment.

“We are losing people, and because Russia attacks, we’re losing people and time, and it’s a pity because our children don’t have real life, childhood, and all the people, to be honest,” he said. “That’s why we need to end this war as quick as possible. I hope that our partners, Americans and Europeans, will help us.”

item.title: Democratic-Aligned Groups Sue Over Federal Crackdown on Voting
item.description:
A coalition of Democratic lawmakers and campaign committees filed a lawsuit on Wednesday asking a federal judge to impose a sweeping halt to efforts by the Trump administration to control various aspects of election administration ahead of next month’s midterm elections, describing a “pattern of intimidation” by the federal government.

The challenge took aim at several federal agencies that the coalition argued were working together to propagate falsehoods about voter fraud to justify new requirements for how states run their elections.

In particular, they asked the judge to block the federal government from ordering states to disqualify individual voters or from directing states to “segregate (and ultimately not count) ballots” from people already registered to vote. They also asked the judge to forbid the administration to threaten to prosecute state or local election officials for conducting routine administration.

The filing came after the Justice Department charged more than two dozen California residents this week with violating federal election laws and filed a lawsuit last week to try to prevent California from counting as many as 20,000 mail-in ballots from people the Department of Homeland Security deemed “likely noncitizens.”

Only U.S. citizens can legally vote in federal elections.

The new Trump efforts have come even as other efforts to catalog instances of voting fraud and seize state voter rolls have repeatedly fallen apart.

“None of this is lawful,” the suit said.

The lawsuit noted President Trump’s long-term fixation on discredited theories about election security. It argued that the Justice Department and the Homeland Security Department had been effectively enlisted in a personal crusade by the president to take over elections, using widespread voter fraud as a pretense.

“For over a decade now, President Donald J. Trump has bombarded the American people with lies and misinformation about American elections and voter fraud,” the group wrote. “While these lies have been debunked at every turn, that has never deterred the president from employing them as a pretext to seize control over elections, even as courts overwhelmingly reject that effort.”

The lawsuit argues that the Trump administration has exceeded its constitutional authority by interfering in the administration of elections, which the Constitution delegates to the states. The case was assigned to Chief Judge James E. Boasberg, who has clashed with the Justice Department under Mr. Trump over its handling of other cases last year.

In a statement, a Justice Department spokesman responded that the agency “enforces federal election law, and election integrity is a top priority.”

“Every action the department has taken to protect the integrity of this year’s elections is grounded in the law and being litigated in open court,” the spokesman added.

Democrats have challenged Mr. Trump’s efforts in various states, including California. But the new suit appears to be an effort to secure a court order blocking federal intervention nationally.

Filed in Federal District Court in Washington, it ticked through a number of federal initiatives it said were all rooted in Mr. Trump’s desire to control voting that so far courts have addressed one by one.

It cites, for instance, the more than 30 lawsuits the Justice Department has filed to individually compel states to turn over their voter rolls for review. Federal judges have rejected the Justice Department’s arguments or dismissed the lawsuits entirely more than two dozen times.

The lawsuit also pointed to efforts by the Homeland Security Department to use federal immigration data to cast doubt on state voter rolls, even though months of federal investigations have turned up vanishingly few instances of noncitizens registered to vote.

In September, the Supreme Court allowed states that were inclined to do so to consult with the agency to check for any noncitizens on their voter registries.

The department has taken steps to compile and send lists of known citizens in each state to state elections officials, despite its own determinations that the lists would most likely contain out-of-date information.

Election officials in California have said in sworn statements that they have examined some of the 20,000 voters flagged by federal officials and found that the list includes errors and that a “high percentage” of the people listed were actually born in the United States.

Mr. Trump has also threatened state officials with investigation. Shortly after the Justice Department filed suit against California last week, he warned on social media that officials risked prosecution if they tabulated ballots submitted by people the federal government had flagged.

“They will all go to jail for a long period of time!!!” he wrote.

“This lawlessness did not arise in a vacuum,” the lawsuit stated. “It comes as courts across the country have broadly enjoined the president’s executive orders concerning elections, forbidden his attempt to nationalize rules for voting by mail and refused his demands that states turn over their unredacted voter rolls.”

item.title: Abdul El-Sayed Confronts Attacks on His Faith and Family Ties
item.description:
In the final weeks of Michigan’s closely watched Senate race, Dr. Abdul El-Sayed’s ethnicity, religion and family have come under renewed attacks and scrutiny.

His Republican opponent, former Representative Mike Rogers, invoked Dr. El-Sayed’s mother during their first debate, trying to draw a connection between her and Al Qaeda. President Trump has mocked the pronunciation of Dr. El-Sayed’s name and has started referring to him by his middle name, Mohamed. And Republican ads have suggested that Dr. El-Sayed has ties to terrorist groups or to the Muslim Brotherhood, the Islamist political movement.

Dr. El-Sayed has forcefully responded to the questions about his identity. Over the weekend, a nearly five-minute exchange at a town-hall event with a man who asked him to “disavow the Muslim Brotherhood” went viral on social media. This week, in a brief, testy interaction with a reporter from Newsmax, he said, “I clearly disavow” the movement. And in a new video, Dr. El-Sayed says that he prays daily and calls himself a “man of faith.”

Now Dr. El-Sayed, who would be the first Muslim senator if he wins, finds himself confronting both ugly attacks and pointed questions about family members — particularly his mother and a half sister — and their past comments and personal histories. Republicans have pushed to make those questions a main story line in the final days of a Senate race that could determine control of the chamber.

The focus on Dr. El-Sayed’s identity, religion and family comes at the end of a campaign defined by its emotional and bitter clashes over Israel and the United States’ role in the Middle East. Dr. El-Sayed has cast himself as a leader of the Democratic Party’s march away from support for Israel, arguing that the longtime U.S. ally should not exist as an explicitly Jewish state and calling for an end to its American military support.

As he approaches a second and final televised debate with Mr. Rogers on Wednesday, Dr. El-Sayed is appealing to voters who are not Muslim to see him as a person of faith whose experience reflects America’s history of religious pluralism.

“A lot of people question whether or not I can win this race because of my name,” he said during a speech this month in Cadillac, Mich. “I’ve been a guy named Abdul Mohamed El-Sayed in Michigan almost my entire life. I would say I’m pretty good at being named Abdul in Michigan.”

The questions that Mr. Rogers is pushing about Dr. El-Sayed’s ties to the Muslim Brotherhood relate in part to an open letter he signed in 2012.

That letter, which Dr. El-Sayed signed while he was in medical school, asked Mohamed Morsi, who was then the new Egyptian president from a party that represented the political wing of the Muslim Brotherhood, to “purge the media and police” of supporters of the dictatorship that had been toppled during the Arab Spring. (Mr. Morsi, Egypt’s first democratically elected president, established good working relations with the United States.)

Dr. El-Sayed’s campaign denied that he had any connection to the Muslim Brotherhood. When asked recently by reporters, he has disavowed the group. His campaign aides declined to answer questions about the 2012 letter.

Many of the Republican attacks on Dr. El-Sayed focus on his mother, Fatten Elkomy, an Egyptian immigrant.

Dr. El-Sayed’s parents separated when he was 3 years old. He was raised in Missouri, Florida and Michigan by his father and stepmother, a Michigan-born descendant of Abigail Adams. He has featured his grandparents in advertisements, including one that began airing on Tuesday in which they declared, “We’re Presbyterians.”

After the separation, Ms. Elkomy lived in Egypt at first and later in Missouri, where she worked for a charity that was designated by the U.S. government as a supporter of terrorist groups, including Al Qaeda.

The charity, the Islamic American Relief Agency, was founded in 1985, raised at least $20 million and funded social services for children in Africa and Asia, according to federal records. It closed in 2004 after the terrorism designation.

The group and several leaders ultimately pleaded guilty — not to supporting terrorism, but to a lesser charge of transferring more than $1 million to Iraq in violation of federal sanctions. Its executive director, Mubarak Hamed, was sentenced in 2012 to nearly five years in prison.

This month, five people involved in the case said in interviews that they did not remember Ms. Elkomy because she was a low-ranking employee and was never accused of wrongdoing.

“She didn’t have anything to do with anything,” said Charles Swift, a lawyer who represented the group.

Among the 945 exhibits cited by prosecutors in a court filing during the case were 13 that pertained to Ms. Elkomy, a detail Republicans have seized on. Most of the exhibits were letters she sent documenting financial transactions between 1999 and 2001. (Records do not include the letters themselves or any information about whether the transactions were illegal.)

Evan Kohlmann, a counterterrorism consultant who was an expert witness in the case, said the charity was so small that all of its employees most likely knew about its activities. He added that the group was part of a global network whose leaders had been found to have previously sent money to Osama bin Laden. “It was no secret that they were doing this,” he said.

The Missouri charity had 14 employees, according to its last tax filing in 2003.

Ms. Elkomy, who now works as a psychiatric nurse practitioner in Missouri, addressed the criminal case years ago in a newspaper interview. She said she had worked at the charity between 1999 and 2004 to serve orphans and had never seen any ties to terrorism.

An even older chapter of Ms. Elkomy’s life has also drawn scrutiny because of years-old posts on social media by her daughter from a marriage after her divorce from Dr. El-Sayed’s father. The daughter, Eman Abdelhadi, who is now a professor at the University of Chicago, posted in 2012: “Had an amazing talk with my mom about her activism in the Muslim Brotherhood during the early 70s while she was in college #respect.” Ms. Elkomy has said she graduated from medical school at Alexandria University in Egypt in 1983.

Dr. Abdelhadi has also made other posts suggesting that family members in Egypt were part of the Muslim Brotherhood. None have mentioned Dr. El-Sayed.

Dr. El-Sayed’s campaign pointed to his past remarks about his complex family dynamics. He wrote in one of his books that his father left Egypt to escape the country’s political oppression and that he had little relationship with his mother. His aides said that any suggestions that he had connections to overseas terrorist groups were racist and Islamophobic.

Dr. El-Sayed’s mother and half sister, with whom he also did not grow up, did not respond to requests for comment. His aides declined a request for an interview with him for this article, and declined to talk in detail about his family or religious practices.

“I was raised here in Michigan, went to the University of Michigan, rebuilt the health department in this city, led the health department in this county, and you want to ask me about what was happening in Egypt in the 1970s?” Dr. El-Sayed, a former public health official, said in a recent interview with NBC. “Are you serious?”

When the general election began, Mr. Rogers accused Dr. El-Sayed of being too far left politically for Michigan. He made a play for disaffected Democrats and described the El-Sayed campaign as “filled with anger, divisiveness, calls for violence and views that are out of touch with your values.”

It was a predictable line of attack against a progressive Democrat who had campaigned with the provocative streamer Hasan Piker during the primary race.

Then came the debate this month.

Mr. Rogers attacked Dr. El-Sayed’s mother and suggested his rival had ties to terrorists. “Well, if you have someone in your family that might be on the, on the watch list —” Mr. Rogers said, before Dr. El-Sayed cut him off.

“You going after my mom?” he asked.

Mr. Rogers stopped, but his allies did not.

Mr. Trump began calling Dr. El-Sayed by his middle name, Mohamed, and mocked the number of syllables in his given name. Ads emerged on television saying that Dr. El-Sayed had “ties to the Islamist movement.” On CNN, Mr. Rogers said his rival had “a long history of supporting the Muslim Brotherhood.” Republican allies of Mr. Rogers stepped up efforts to scrutinize Dr. El-Sayed’s political allies and donors.

This push came to a head on Saturday night when, at a town hall in Caro, a small town in northeast Michigan, a man who was reportedly a Republican operative asked Dr. El-Sayed if he would disavow the Muslim Brotherhood.

Dr. El-Sayed’s campaign was so pleased with his response — “Sure, yes, absolutely,” followed by a colloquy about the Constitution and his loyalty to it — that it posted the exchange on social media, where it spread widely.

Republicans argued that Dr. El-Sayed had bullied the questioner, and kept pushing the discussion about the candidate’s faith.

On Monday, Dr. El-Sayed posted a video that showed images of churches and a menorah while portraying himself as another religiously observant person.

“I pray every day,” he said. “We need a few more people of faith in Washington. I’m Abdul El-Sayed, man of faith.”

From the start, Dr. El-Sayed had few illusions about the role his faith and ethnicity would play in his Senate campaign. Many other Muslim candidates for lower-profile offices had faced baseless accusations of mixed allegiances or ties to terrorist groups.

“We kind of all knew where this was headed,” Dr. El-Sayed said in an interview after his campaign event this month in Cadillac.

Dr. El-Sayed wrote in his 2020 memoir, “Healing Politics,” that he was “raised in a conservative Muslim household.” He went to Sunday school, fasted during Ramadan and refrained from eating pork.

And in interviews, he has said he attends a mosque, prays five times a day and does not drink alcohol. At Michigan, he was president of the Muslim Students Association and married his wife while they were undergraduates.

“I believe in an Islam that emphasizes God and my responsibility in his creation,” he wrote. “The Islam I practice doesn’t judge people; it seeks to empathize with and empower them.”

For a while during his Senate race, Dr. El-Sayed ran advertisements stressing his guy-next-door bona fides. He was captain of his high school football team and gave a commencement speech upon graduating from the University of Michigan.

For other Muslim elected officials, Dr. El-Sayed’s experience in recent weeks is reminiscent of what they have gone through in their campaigns.

Sam Rasoul, a Palestinian American who has been in the Virginia House of Delegates since 2014, was asked during a televised debate when he ran for lieutenant governor in 2021 if campaign donations he received from Muslims meant he would be loyal to all of Virginia.

Four years later, a different Muslim candidate, Ghazala Hashmi, was elected as Virginia’s lieutenant governor after facing similar attacks. She said she had texted with Dr. El-Sayed during his Senate campaign to offer encouragement.

“There’s such a heightened level of anti-Muslim rhetoric that has grown over the past couple of decades,” said Ms. Hashmi, who is now one of two Muslims who hold statewide office in the United States. “Islamophobia is something that is a part of the political system here.”

Onstage at campaign events, Dr. El-Sayed often stands not in front of signs with his campaign logo, as he frequently did during the primary, but in front of a giant American flag. He proactively talks about what Mr. Trump, Vice President JD Vance, Mr. Rogers and others are saying about him.

“They think my name and my faith are enough to get people to stop paying attention to the issues,” he said this month in Ionia. “My name is not the reason you can’t afford gas. My name’s not the reason you can’t afford your groceries.”

Susan C. Beachy contributed research.

item.title: Vance Defends Ramaswamy’s Ad as Backlash Threatens Ohio Campaign
item.description:
Vice President JD Vance on Wednesday defended an ad featuring the estranged mother of the Democrat running for Ohio governor, Amy Acton, dismissing condemnation of it from even fellow Republicans as “whining.”

In the ad from Vivek Ramaswamy, Dr. Acton’s Republican opponent, the mother said her daughter had lied and exaggerated about her childhood struggles. The ad was met with outrage, given that the mother’s longtime husband, Dr. Acton’s stepfather, was charged with raping the candidate when she was 12, according to records produced by the Acton campaign.

Mr. Ramaswamy is putting $4 million behind the spot. Mr. Vance lauded it, saying it “calls it out like it is, and calls Amy Acton a liar.”

Child sexual abuse has been a surprisingly prevalent issue in the 2026 midterms. It has surfaced in Texas, where Democrats accused Attorney General Ken Paxton of treating a convicted abuser leniently; in Kansas, where Republicans said the Democratic candidate for Senate, Adam Hamilton, failed to respond to abuse accusations by a volunteer at his church; and in multiple races where Republican votes against releasing the Epstein files have become political fodder.

Even though Mr. Ramaswamy’s ad does not directly mention sexual abuse, it has brought it to the forefront of the Ohio governor’s race and whipped up national attention. In the ad, Donna Arthur, Dr. Acton’s mother, accused her daughter of lying about details she has relayed about a troubled childhood in which she was homeless for a time. During that period, Dr. Acton has said, she was sexually abused by her stepfather. She has said she and her mother have not spoken since she was 12, when Ms. Arthur lost custody of both her daughter and her son.

Documents provided by the Acton campaign this week show that a grand jury had indicted the candidate’s stepfather on charges of raping Dr. Acton in 1978, the year Ms. Arthur lost custody. The stepfather, Cledith Arthur, pleaded not guilty, and then fled the state before trial. He died in Pennsylvania in 2004.

This week, Dr. Acton’s campaign decried the ad and quickly responded with one of its own, in which her brother, Philip Stearns, says that she had for years been the victim of their stepfather’s physical and sexual abuse.

Asked Wednesday evening about the ad, President Trump tried three approaches. He first claimed not to know anything about it. Then he cited its contents at length, saying, “It’s a very unusual situation to have a mother hate a daughter that much.” Finally, he absolved Mr. Ramaswamy of responsibility for it, concluding, “I don’t think that has anything to do with Vivek.”

Mr. Vance, at a Wednesday morning campaign rally in the state, lauded Mr. Ramaswamy for the spot even as the backlash threatened to engulf the candidate’s campaign.

“I’m a little bit disgusted when I see Republicans across the country who are whining more about that advertisement than they are about what the congressional Democrats and other Democrats want to do to the United States of America,” Mr. Vance told reporters. “So I would say to Ohio Republicans, do you actually think that Amy Acton is unfit to serve as governor of the state of Ohio? I do.”

The downplaying of the ad’s significance by the president and vice president did little to stem the criticism.

MK Pritzker, the wife of Illinois’s Democratic governor, JB Pritzker, announced on Wednesday that she would put half a million dollars behind Dr. Acton’s campaign, accusing Mr. Ramaswamy of exploiting “a highly qualified woman’s pain for political gain.”

The editorial board of The Columbus Dispatch announced its backing for Dr. Acton for governor on Wednesday morning, describing the ad in its endorsement as “revolting and unsettling.”

Multiple well-known figures in the Ohio Republican establishment either criticized the ad or distanced themselves from it. They include Frank LaRose, the Ohio secretary of state; Lydia Mihalik, director of the Ohio Department of Development; Ryan Smith, the Republican former speaker of the Ohio House; and Senator Jon Husted. In a statement, Mr. Husted, who is in the middle of a tight battle for his Senate seat, said, “I would not have run that ad.”

But denunciations also came from people far outside of establishment circles. Casey Putsch, a car designer who ran against Mr. Ramaswamy from the hard right in the Republican primary, slammed the ad on social media and said that he would vote for Dr. Acton. Mr. Ramaswamy and his campaign, he wrote, are “attacking Amy Acton over the abuse she endured as a child.”

With Election Day less than two weeks away, erosion of support from the Republicans’ Ohio establishment and its far right could spell trouble for Mr. Ramaswamy.

Kathy Barnette, a conservative radio host who advised Mr. Ramaswamy’s presidential campaign, said that the stakes of the election could not be higher and that she could vouch “100 percent” for Mr. Ramaswamy’s character and vision. At the same time, Ms. Barnette, who said her mother was raped at a young age, called the ad a “very personal thing” for her.

“It is a very fine line that the Ramaswamy campaign are walking in sharing this information,” she said. “They’re taking a huge bet.”

Did she think it was a bet worth taking? “No comment,” she said.

AdImpact, a political ad-watching firm, said Wednesday that the Ramaswamy campaign added $2.8 million in advertising reservations to the nearly $15 million already in place.

Some Republicans said the angry reaction to the ad was more political than genuine, much of it coming from people who did not support Mr. Ramaswamy in the first place.

“This was a bold and raw move, but many of the critics of this ad have strong political motivations to launch their criticism,” said Mark R. Weaver, a Republican political consultant in Ohio.

At a rally at a convention center near Cincinnati that was headlined by Mr. Vance, at which Mr. Ramaswamy briefly spoke, attendees brushed off the criticism. Some said that Dr. Acton’s mother was entitled to give her side of the story, while others downplayed the whole controversy.

“We are not voting for ads, we are voting for people,” said Greg Garland, who was attending with a group of people supporting the Republican ticket.

On Tuesday night, after being heckled about the ad, Mr. Ramaswamy told reporters, “I would love for this race, this election, to be about the substantive issues that impact Ohioans. Unfortunately, Amy Acton has been hiding from those issues.”

Kevin Williams contributed reporting from Cincinnati.

item.title: A.I. Discovered a Critical Security Flaw Underpinning Websites
item.description:
Security researchers using OpenAI’s advanced artificial intelligence models unearthed major bugs in a piece of software used widely across the internet, setting off fears around the world about significant disruptions for consumers and businesses.

The Trump administration and some governments in Europe and Asia warned that all organizations that rely on the software, which is known as PHP, should immediately install updates released Wednesday to patch the flaws. By some estimates, about 70 percent of all websites and web applications use the software. Recent data suggests its adoption is waning.

While the fixes are readily available, their public release creates a kind of road map for hackers, who could easily reverse engineer the patches in order to initiate attacks before businesses, governments and people can protect their systems. Successful attacks could allow hackers to take control of servers, steal private data and deface websites, experts said.

Security agencies, including the National Security Agency, advised companies to take their systems offline if a patch could not be immediately applied, an effort to prevent hackers from attacking. Some government sites in Europe took those steps, rendering some services unavailable.

The disclosure further heightened concerns that have been building over the last six months about A.I.’s potential to upend cybersecurity unless security shortcomings are addressed.

“We have an urgent request for everyone to take action tonight,” Sanae Takaichi, the prime minister of Japan, said on social media. “If it is difficult to apply the fix patch promptly, temporarily suspending websites and similar measures can be considered an effective way to reduce risk.”

PHP is an open-source programming language that helps run website and internet applications. The nonprofit foundation that oversees PHP released a patch Wednesday morning, and security experts said that correctly applying the fix should protect websites from harm. But companies big and small, especially those with short-staffed security teams, can often be slow to adopt new patches.

Those kinds of delays, the widespread use of PHP and the ease with which hackers can move to target many organizations have prompted security professionals to warn that the fallout could be significant.

“With A.I., patching is now an emergency,” said Cynthia Kaiser, a former senior F.B.I. official who oversaw cybersecurity cases and now works at the technology company Halcyon.

The researchers who discovered the bugs work at Calif, a small U.S.-based company of cybersecurity experts who test cutting-edge A.I. models to see what kind of cyberattacks they can identify and build. Their efforts help alert network defenders to undetected problems in order to fix them before malicious hackers can do damage.

Calif said that it discovered the PHP bugs in only a matter of days. Its researchers used GPT-5.6 Sol for the initial findings, and an unreleased OpenAI model for the exploitation of the flaws.

Security researchers said the flaw was concerning given the pervasiveness of the software. In a blog post, OpenAI confirmed that Calif had used its models, and that Wiz, another security company owned by Google, had also independently discovered and reported the vulnerabilities.

“Given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory,” OpenAI said. “It highlights how A.I. can uncover security flaws with internet-scale impact, but the same capabilities can also help attackers rapidly develop offensive tools and exploits.”

The PHP problem was just the latest discovery by Calif, which is among a select group of companies, government agencies and research organizations given early access to advanced A.I. models before they are released publicly. Earlier this year, Calif developed a worm in China’s WeChat communications platform that could have allowed a hacker to rapidly compromise virtually any WeChat account just by calling it. It also used an early version of the Mythos model to bypass security protocols in Apple’s macOS operating system, long viewed as highly secure and difficult to breach.

Those discoveries were relatively contained in their real-world consequences. But the PHP flaws could create lingering problems because of how hackers can recreate the attack and the ubiquity of the software at issue. PHP is a decades-old language that was shorthand for “Personal Home Page,” and is a critical ingredient in popular services like WordPress and Drupal.

Still, data from Shodan, a search engine that scans computer systems across the globe to identify the technologies they run, shows that the adoption of PHP is declining. Many newer websites are built using technologies not vulnerable to this attack.

But some security experts said the bug was potentially one of the most serious found in recent memory, and one of the most significant to date identified by A.I.

“It is certainly one of the most critical bugs of the year,” said Bruce Dang, a researcher at Calif, adding that “the impact will be felt for a while.”

Aaron Krolik contributed reporting from New York.

item.title: A Democratic Candidate for Governor Is Traversing Alaska to Flip the State
item.description:
Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins is on the verge of upending Alaska’s political landscape. But when he entered the race for governor of the red-leaning state earlier this year, he wasn’t even the leading Democrat.

That was Tom Begich, a former state lawmaker and a member of Alaska’s most famous political family. But sometimes, maybe only in a state as geographically vast and electorally small as Alaska, politics really does come down to who works the hardest. And Mr. Kreiss-Tomkins had a plan from the beginning, calculating how many voters he needed to meet to finish first in the state’s crowded open primary.

It was essentially the same strategy he employed in 2012, when he dropped out of Yale at 23 to run for the State Legislature. Back then, he had “a pair of running shoes and a ferry schedule” for southeastern Alaska. He won by 32 votes.

This time, he scaled up, traveling hundreds of miles by boat along the Kuskokwim and Yukon rivers, crossing the Interior by snow machine and taking float planes to as many remote villages as possible. It’s really the only path Democrats have to win statewide in a place where Republicans outnumber them and tend to be concentrated in the relatively accessible Railbelt — Anchorage, the Mat-Su Valley and the Kenai Peninsula.

This year’s race will most likely be won by more than 32 votes, but it might come down to a few thousand or even a few hundred: Around 285,000 Alaskans are expected to vote. Mr. Kreiss-Tomkins’s three opponents are Republican, but unaffiliated voters make up 60 percent of the electorate.

Mr. Kreiss-Tomkins’s voter-engagement effort is one reason Democrats see an opening to win the Alaska governor’s race for the first time since 1998. Republican infighting is the other.

Twelve Republicans ran in Alaska’s open, top-four primary in August, collectively winning about 49 percent of the vote — more than the two leading Democrats combined. But while the Democrats united behind Mr. Kreiss-Tomkins after he finished first in the primary, Republicans went in the opposite direction.

Bernadette Wilson, a conservative activist and businesswoman, finished ahead of the other Republicans, and has led them in fund-raising. But former Mayor Dave Bronson of Anchorage and former Attorney General Treg Taylor have resisted calls to unite behind her.

Lately, the Republicans have begun attacking one another. Mr. Bronson has raised questions about unpaid debts and lawsuits involving Ms. Wilson’s waste management company, while Ms. Wilson has accused him of putting himself ahead of the party. Mr. Bronson recently told The Anchorage Daily News that Republican leaders should have done more to vet candidates and narrow the field. “We just failed as a party,” he said.

The three Republican candidates for governor were each hoping for President Trump’s help, even as polls showed his popularity slipping while the cost of oil rose in a state he carried three times.

All three candidates skipped recent debates to attend Alaska rallies by Vice President JD Vance and Mr. Trump. Only Ms. Wilson got what she wanted: Mr. Trump endorsed her, demanded that Mr. Taylor and Mr. Bronson drop out and attacked ranked-choice voting, which he has called crooked.

But it’s too late to take their names off the ballot. And Mr. Trump’s complaints about ranked-choice voting could help Mr. Kreiss-Tomkins if it inspires some Republicans to rank only Ms. Wilson.

Under Alaska’s system, candidates with the fewest votes are eliminated in successive rounds, with their supporters’ ballots transferred to the next-ranked choices.

Ballots that list no backup candidate are “exhausted” when their first choice is eliminated. So if enough Republicans rank only Ms. Wilson and she is eliminated before another Republican, those votes would be lost to the remaining candidates — potentially depriving a Republican opponent of the support needed to overcome Mr. Kreiss-Tomkins and the base he spent months traveling the state to build.

item.title: Cornell Case Highlights Shifting Federal Title IX Enforcement
item.description:
After President Richard M. Nixon signed Title IX into law in 1972, the federal civil rights law banning sex discrimination in education came to be viewed as a potent tool to expand the participation of girls and women in sports.

Four decades later, a student-led movement opposing gender-based violence on college campuses spurred the Obama administration to use the law to pressure universities to crack down on sexual assault.

Fast-forward another 15 years, and President Trump is again deploying the broad powers of Title IX — pulling back the focus on sexual misconduct and instead dismantling protections for transgender students.

The divergent priorities show how ideologies of different presidents have shaped federal enforcement of Title IX, a landmark civil rights law receiving renewed attention after a Cornell University student alleged that she was sexually assaulted by multiple members of a fraternity. The law’s broad statutory language has enabled successive administrations to reinterpret its scope — and rewrite enforcement guidelines — with each shift in the cultural landscape, including the #MeToo movement and its subsequent backlash.

College officials say the swinging pendulum of federal enforcement has created confusion on campuses, sowing doubt among students considering whether to report incidents.

“I have heard from students that they are unsure or even scared about reporting to their school’s Title IX office to begin with, for fear of a retraumatizing process that will not be supportive,” said Emma Grasso Levine, senior manager of Know Your IX, a youth-led victims’ rights group.

Title IX requires that schools establish a process outside of criminal courts to determine responsibility for sexual misconduct, impose discipline and provide support services that restore a survivor’s right to equal access to education.

The allegation of a gang rape at Cornell in 2024 resulted in expulsions for two students and lighter punishments for others, according to records of the school’s Title IX investigation that were obtained by The New York Times. Last month, the former student, known as Jane Doe, sued the school and others, arguing that Cornell failed to enforce its procedures for responding to allegations of sexual violence.

Jane Doe’s lawyer, Thomas P. Giuffra, told The Times in an email that she dropped out in February 2025 after seeing the students she had accused on campus and fearing that others involved might be in her classes. None of the accused men have been charged with a crime, and all have denied wrongdoing.

Michael Kotlikoff, the president of Cornell, said last week in an interview with The Times that he should have been told that Jane Doe had dropped out. Earlier this month, Cornell named Sally Yates, a former acting attorney general, to review the university’s handling of the allegations under Title IX and other federal and state laws.

“If, in fact, a student has withdrawn because she feels unsafe at the outcome of the Title IX process or there is specific concerns around the individuals — you know, there were no-contact orders for those individuals — I think that’s something that leadership should be made aware of,” Dr. Kotlikoff said.

Title IX was passed as part of an enormous education bill in 1972. In an article explaining the legislation’s major provisions published at the time, The New York Times listed the ban on sex discrimination as the 11th item. President Nixon’s signing statement did not mention Title IX.

But the law took years to fully take shape. Initially, Title IX forced universities to dismantle sex-based admissions caps and expand women’s sports.

The phrase “sexual harassment” was not coined until 1975, when an instructor at Cornell, Lin Farley, spoke out about female students and staff being fired, demoted or forced to quit because of unwanted advances from male bosses and co-workers. Two years later, federal courts started allowing cases of sexual harassment under Title IX.

For the next three decades, Republican and Democratic administrations told schools that Title IX banned sexual harassment. But women’s rights activists and campus protesters increasingly complained that federal oversight was lax.

After Delta Kappa Epsilon pledges at Yale University marched across campus in 2010 chanting, “No means yes; yes means anal,” activists cited the episode to argue that the threat of sexual assault created a hostile learning environment for women.

In 2011, Russlynn Ali, President Barack Obama’s head of the Education Department’s Office for Civil Rights, issued a 19-page public letter stating that sexual violence and harassment created an environment so hostile that they jeopardized women’s access to education and violated Title IX.

The letter required schools to adopt procedures to file complaints, designate an official to coordinate Title IX compliance and put in place sexual harassment training programs.

The letter also said schools should evaluate complaints based on a “preponderance of evidence,” a standard of proof that means it was more likely than not that sexual harassment had occurred. Some schools at the time used the higher “clear and convincing” standard of proof.

Catherine E. Lhamon, who succeeded Ms. Ali as the Education Department’s top civil rights lawyer, threatened to strip federal funding from universities that failed to adequately respond to sexual misconduct allegations.

More than a decade later, lawyers and university officials interviewed for this article recalled Ms. Lhamon’s description of the “huge hammer” she could use to force compliance.

Asked about those comments, Ms. Lhamon said, “That sounds exactly like me.”

“I was very comfortable withholding funds from universities that violated the law,” said Ms. Lhamon, now the executive director of the Edley Center on Law and Democracy at the University of California, Berkeley.

“But this was not political for me,” she continued. “It did not matter — red or blue state, red or blue jurisdiction. If you were violating the law and would not come into compliance, this was the lever we had to enforce. It was, 100 percent, something I was very serious about.”

But a backlash was underway, with legal scholars, civil liberties groups and faculty associations warning that due process rights were being eroded.

From 2011 to 2020, students filed more than 700 lawsuits claiming universities had mishandled cases in which they had been accused of sexual misconduct, according to a database maintained by Jonathan Taylor, whose group, Title IX for All, advises students accused of violating sexual misconduct policies.

“What we have learned from these lawsuits is that we unfortunately can’t trust universities to do the right thing,” Mr. Taylor said. “They will misrepresent what people say; they will not gather the evidence that they should be gathering; and they won’t put some evidence into the investigation record.”

Mr. Trump, whose first presidential campaign weathered a political storm over an “Access Hollywood” video of him talking about grabbing women without consent — which he dismissed as “locker room talk” — rescinded Ms. Ali’s letter during the first year of his first term.

His administration also rewrote Title IX regulations. Rather than issue a letter, Betsy DeVos, then the education secretary, oversaw an extensive rule-making effort that codified the changes in federal regulations.

“The era of rule by letter is over,” Ms. DeVos said in a speech in 2017. “Through intimidation and coercion, this failed system has clearly pushed schools to overreach.”

The result was a 554-page addition to the Federal Register that provided more protections for the accused. Enacted in 2020, the rule replaced administrative reviews with courtroom-style proceedings that required live hearings in which the accused and accuser could see and hear each other. Lawyers for both sides could present evidence and cross-examine witnesses.

The Trump administration has said the rule ensures fairness, while opponents argue it created an onerous, intimidating environment for victims.

President Joseph R. Biden Jr.’s administration attempted to overhaul those rules again.

But it did not adopt a new rule until 2024, when it was immediately challenged in court. A federal judge blocked the move in 2025, after Mr. Trump had returned to power, and the Republican administration did not appeal the ruling.

Last month, Mr. Trump’s Education Department formally repealed the Biden rule and restored the 2020 standard. Education Secretary Linda McMahon said in a statement at the time that the change “faithfully reflects court orders and congressional intent — reducing confusion for parents, students and educational institutions.”

The department is also considering another change that would amend Title IX regulations to incorporate Mr. Trump’s executive order last year that defined “sex” as only male or female.

Civil rights lawyers from both Republican and Democratic administrations called on Congress to clarify Title IX and prevent continued enforcement shifts but disagreed sharply over what those changes should look like — and who was to blame for weaponizing the ban on sex discrimination.

“The back-and-forth over Title IX is an extreme form of what I call regulatory whiplash,” said Kenneth L. Marcus, who was the Education Department’s top civil rights lawyer during Mr. Trump’s first administration. “This is not good for anyone. It reduces consistency, predictability and evenhandedness.”

Chantelle Botticelli, a former New York sex crimes prosecutor who has worked on Title IX issues for universities, including Cornell, said the shifts have been disruptive for students and administrators.

“There’s an erosion of the trust that folks in this space have worked really hard to build over the last decade,” said Ms. Botticelli, now a Title IX consultant with Grand River Solutions.

Scott Schneider, who advises on sex discrimination cases and trains law enforcement on sexual assault investigations, said both sides of the aisle bear some responsibility.

“The public conversation gets dominated by ideologues on both sides of the political spectrum — and the part that waxes and wanes is who has the most influence,” Mr. Schneider said. “I don’t think either one has had a lot of concern for the other side of this, and it shows.”

Debra Kamin contributed reporting.
