item.title: Discovery of New Fake Polls Puts a Spotlight on Trust in Surveys
item.description:
The pollster had been releasing surveys since June, shifting from one midterm battleground to another: Michigan. Maine. Kansas.

On Tuesday night, after the polling website FiftyPlusOne contacted the pollster, Wedgewood Polls, with questions about the authenticity of its surveys, the team behind the supposed data firm acknowledged that almost all of its work was fake. The whole thing, Wedgewood claimed, was an “experimental project.”

The fake polls were highlighted by well-known polling aggregators, including on the pages The New York Times uses to track surveys published by outside pollsters in key midterm races. The Times removed those polls Tuesday night and published an editors’ note that said it had included the Wedgewood polls — 15 in all — after the pollster answered a series of detailed questions from The Times about the pollsters’ identities, methods and funding.

It was the second time this year that fake polls have become news in the political world, underscoring the risks of misleading or false polling in an era of little-known data firms, hard-to-reach voters and suddenly ubiquitous prediction markets. It comes amid broader scrutiny of the way candidates have increasingly sought to use — or create — unreliable polling to serve their purposes, as well as larger questions over whether traditional polling can be trusted after high-profile misses.

In August, a group behind a different set of bogus polls in California, Nevada and Wisconsin said that they had published them as a “social experiment.”

Wedgewood echoed that language.

“How easy is it for an entirely fabricated polling firm to gain traction, be taken seriously, and expose how little scrutinization exists in media and in public commentary?” the supposed firm wrote in a statement it posted on social media. “The short answer: Far too easy.”

While Wedgewood claimed that it was all a ploy, the effort seemed to involve a lot of work.

The group posted survey documents on a website and on social media, which it has since removed. It also made at least three appeals on social media for funding or sponsorship to cover its activities. On Tuesday night, it posted that one of its polls — a survey in Nebraska — was “real.”

FiftyPlusOne, a polling website run by former employees of FiveThirtyEight, wrote on Tuesday night that it had reached out to Wedgewood with a request for comment earlier that day. That website had essentially sought to replicate one of Wedgewood’s polls in Mississippi, which Wedgewood has said was conducted with an online survey platform called Pollfish, after it noticed inconsistencies in Wedgewood’s data. That exercise, FiftyPlusOne wrote, made it “clear that the red flags we had seen in the Wedgewood data were definitely still waving.”

“It’s getting easier to conduct low-quality polls — or fake them altogether,” FiftyPlusOne wrote.

On Wednesday morning, a link to the website for Wedgewood Polls generated an error. An email message bounced back.

The Times listed Wedgewood’s polls on its tracking pages for the states and congressional districts the group had purported to survey. It did not claim to have produced national surveys of generic ballots, nor of President Trump’s approval rating.

The Wedgewood findings had no bearing on The Times’s own polling operation, which works in partnership with the Siena Research Institute.

The polls, which were shared on social media by other polling aggregators, helped shape the perception of the races they purported to cover, even among the candidates themselves.

After a Wedgewood poll in June showed her support in the single digits, Mallory McMorrow, a Michigan state senator who was running in the state’s Democratic primary for the U.S. Senate, said donations dried up and her campaign’s volunteers were left bereft.

“I felt like I had let so many of them down,” Ms. McMorrow wrote on social media on Tuesday night. The Wedgewood poll, she wrote, came on the heels of a different poll that showed her trailing, though it was ultimately spiked after her campaign raised concerns about it. (Other polls at the time showed her support declining, too.)

“It was a one-two punch,” she wrote, that “killed us.”

Last week in Mississippi, the campaign for Scott Colom, the Democratic nominee for Senate, trumpeted a fake finding from Wedgewood in a news release, citing it as evidence of Mr. Colom’s “massive momentum.”

item.title: A Bush Brother Breaks Ranks to Vote for Talarico
item.description:
Neil M. Bush, a brother of former President George W. Bush, said Tuesday that he had voted for James Talarico, the Democratic nominee in the Senate race in Texas, and expressed serious concerns about the record of the scandal-plagued Republican candidate, Ken Paxton.

Mr. Bush, a son of President George H.W. Bush whose family has deep ties to Texas Republicans, wrote on Facebook that his decision to vote early for the Democrat had been motivated by “deep concern about Ken Paxton’s record and genuine admiration for the character and principles I see in James Talarico.” The New York Times confirmed that the post was authentic.

It was a remarkable announcement from someone whose brother served as the Republican governor of Texas and whose father had been a two-term Republican congressman from Texas.

“I have been deeply troubled by Paxton’s conduct as Texas Attorney General, particularly his decision to challenge the results of the 2020 presidential election in other states in an effort to help Donald Trump remain in power,” wrote Mr. Bush, 71. “I believe that effort was an affront to our democratic institutions and the peaceful transfer of power. My concerns about his judgment and conduct are hardly mine alone. He was impeached by the Republican-controlled Texas House, although subsequently acquitted by the Texas Senate.”Mr. Paxton, aided by a late endorsement from President Trump, won the Republican nomination for Senate in Texas by defeating Senator John Cornyn, a longtime pillar of the Republican establishment in Texas.

Mr. Bush said his vote was more than a protest against Mr. Paxton or Mr. Trump’s leadership of the Republican Party, writing that he had been “enormously impressed” by Mr. Talarico, a Texas state lawmaker and Presbyterian seminarian.

“I see in him the qualities I admire most in public servants: integrity, civility, humility, and a willingness to listen to those with whom he disagrees,” Mr. Bush wrote.

Mr. Bush added that he remained deeply invested “in many traditional Republican principles,” but that “character matters more than party affiliation.”

Mr. Paxton’s campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Former President George W. Bush has not weighed in on the Senate race. His daughter Barbara Bush donated to a super PAC behind Mr. Talarico, according to campaign finance filings. (She had also knocked on doors for Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential race.)

Theodore Schleifer contributed reporting.

item.title: Pro-Israel Lobby Puts Late Money Behind Republican to Thwart El-Sayed
item.description:
The country’s leading pro-Israel lobby has quietly made a major last-minute donation to support Mike Rogers, the Republican candidate for Senate in Michigan. His opponent, Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, is a vocal critic of Israel whom the group spent heavily to try to defeat in the Democratic primary.

The group, the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, has almost never backed a Republican in a competitive general election race. But it has started contributing in recent days to a pro-Rogers super PAC, and plans to give as much as $9 million, according to two people with knowledge of the plans who shared them under condition of anonymity because the spending was not meant to be immediately disclosed.

The donation comes after initial skepticism from the Rogers campaign about tying itself to AIPAC, whose support became an explosive issue in Democratic primary elections this year. At a debate on Oct. 8, however, Mr. Rogers opened to door for AIPAC’s engagement by responding to a question that he would “take all of that help.”

The donation went to the Great Lakes Conservatives Fund, a group exclusively focused on supporting Mr. Rogers, and was made after an Oct. 14 deadline that would have required it to be disclosed before Election Day. On Friday, the super PAC disclosed that it was making a $4.6 million media buy in Michigan.

AIPAC declined to comment on its spending in the race. The Rogers super PAC did not respond to a request for comment.

Several of the super PAC’s new spots target the Muslim background of Dr. El-Sayed, raising questions about his loyalty to Egypt and whether he has ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamist group with ties to extremists. He has denied any ties and dismissed the suggestion as part of a series of Islamophobic attacks.

AIPAC faces growing animosity in the Democratic Party — and even among some Republicans — for its staunch support of Israel at a time when a growing number of Americans object to the war in Gaza. Dr. El-Sayed turned the group’s support of his primary opponent, Representative Haley Stevens, into a central campaign issue.

The New York Times reported in August that Mr. Rogers had some reservations about AIPAC again spending heavily to defeat Dr. El-Sayed, worrying that it could backfire with voters. AIPAC’s super PAC has made disclosed expenditures of less than $300,000 in the last three weeks in Michigan, sending pieces of direct mail to Jewish voters in the state.

Separately on Wednesday, AIPAC announced some changes around the edges of its political operations. The group will no longer offer direct endorsements or donations from its federal PAC. It will continue to operate United Democracy Project, the super PAC that has spent about $85 million in congressional elections this cycle.

Though AIPAC backs many Democrats, the group’s strongest supporters and donors see Dr. El-Sayed’s candidacy as a major threat to Israel’s backing in Congress and support within the Democratic Party. Dr. El-Sayed has said he opposes Israel’s right to exist as an explicitly Jewish state, angering many Jewish leaders.

The day after Dr. El-Sayed’s primary win, Bernie Kaminetsky, AIPAC’s president, wrote to supporters that the group maintained a “principled opposition to the dangerous policies El-Sayed wants to bring to the U.S. Senate.”

item.title: Gambling Hotline Ex-Director Stole $1.5M to Feed Betting Habit, Prosecutors Say
item.description:
A former director of Florida’s problem gambling hotline was sentenced last week to nearly 10 years in prison after prosecutors said he stole nearly $1.5 million from a previous employer to feed his gambling habit.

The man, Philip L. Sullivan, 43, of Panama City, Fla., took the job in March 2025, a year after he was arrested on grand larceny charges. He said he wanted to help others who struggle with compulsive gambling.

He “quickly became an invaluable asset to the organization,” Jennifer Kruse, the executive director of the Florida Council on Compulsive Gambling, which runs the hotline, wrote in July in a letter to the judge overseeing Mr. Sullivan’s criminal case.

By his own count, Mr. Sullivan said he had counseled more than 460 people who had called the 24-hour hotline while his case was playing out in state court.

“If they feel like they’ve gotten something out of a conversation with me, it has given me greater purpose than I feel like I’ve ever had in my life,” Mr. Sullivan said two weeks ago, as he was awaiting sentencing, in an emotional interview on “The Addicted Recovery Show,” a podcast about gambling addiction.

On the podcast, Mr. Sullivan said he started betting on football and “March Madness” college basketball when he was in his 20s, and then expanded into gambling on hockey, baseball and tennis.

Eventually, he took out loans, including one in his wife’s name, to feed his habit. He also started taking high doses of the stimulant medication Adderall, which he had been prescribed for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. That led to “a very compulsive routine,” where he would wake up, take Adderall and start placing sports bets, he said.

Prosecutors said that, beginning in April 2023, Mr. Sullivan took $1.47 million from Royal American Companies, a Florida company that builds and manages housing, where he was the vice president of accounting.

He used his Royal American credit card to buy thousands of gift cards, prosecutors said, and then sold the cards online for a percentage of their value in cryptocurrency. He then took the cryptocurrency and gambled with it online, where he lost a majority of it, prosecutors said.

Mr. Sullivan said that at one point he was placing single bets of up to $50,000.

His theft wasn’t discovered until March 2024, when the credit cards at Royal American started to be declined because of outstanding balances, prosecutors said. When Mr. Sullivan was confronted by his boss, he started deleting files from his computer and told colleagues and superiors that he had taken the money because someone online was extorting him, prosecutors said.

It wasn’t until after Mr. Sullivan was arrested in March 2024 that he fully explained his theft, prosecutors said.

“It winds up being $1.4 million, but 1.2 of that happened in a four-month period, as I tried to win enough to cover things up to get the money put back in place,” Mr. Sullivan said on the podcast. “There was never any capacity to get it under control,” he added, “but when I realized the enormity of the situation, that just made my gambling more compulsive.”

On Friday, Mr. Sullivan pleaded no contest to six counts of grand larceny. Judge Timothy Register of the 14th Judicial Circuit Court of Florida sentenced him to just over nine years and 10 months in prison. Mr. Sullivan was immediately taken into custody.

Prosecutors had asked for a 12-year sentence.

“Any sentence that doesn’t involve incarceration would almost pre-bless the next thief, and would say, ‘Hey, it’s OK to steal more than $1 million from your employer because if you do, there are no consequences,’” prosecutors wrote in a court filing.

Mr. Sullivan’s wife, Mallory Sullivan, said in an interview on Wednesday that the family had hoped that Mr. Sullivan would be sentenced to probation. The couple have two sons, who are 6 and 12, and Mr. Sullivan had no prior criminal record, she said.

“It was definitely a shock to us; we thought they would be reasonable,” she said of the nearly 10-year sentence. “What justice are we doing in society to put a man in prison who is actively engaged with recovery efforts?”

After he was arrested, Mr. Sullivan contacted the nonprofit Florida Council on Compulsive Gambling and asked if he could volunteer.

“You want there to be something positive that you can derive from this experience that you’ve gone through, and the hurt you’ve caused other people,” Mr. Sullivan said on the podcast.

The council told him that, because of the high rate of relapse associated with compulsive gambling, he would need to go a full year without gambling before he could be considered as a volunteer.

But he impressed Ms. Kruse, the council’s executive director, enough that she hired him as the hotline director when he made it to that one-year milestone.

Ms. Kruse, who did not respond to messages on Wednesday, said in her letter that she hoped Judge Register would consider the progress Mr. Sullivan had made when deciding on his sentence.

“His journey reflects not just recovery but meaningful transformation, from someone impacted by addiction to someone deeply invested in helping others avoid similar harm,” she wrote.

Kitty Bennett contributed research.

item.title: New Rules in North Carolina Threaten Thousands of Mail Ballots
item.description:
New mail ballot rules in North Carolina may lead to the rejection of thousands of ballots, left-leaning voting rights groups warned this week. The groups urged voters to check the status of their mail ballot or vote in person to make sure their votes count.

At issue is a requirement that voters seal not only the outer envelope of their mail ballot but also an inner envelope that contains the ballot itself.

Two groups, Common Cause North Carolina and the Southern Coalition for Social Justice, tracked data from 27 of the state’s 100 counties and found a higher ballot rejection rate than in past elections, mostly because of unsealed inner envelopes. The rejection rate is at about 3 percent statewide, the groups found, though it was two or three times as high as in some larger counties.

More ballots being rejected could prove decisive in a state that is known for its razor-thin election margins and that this year is also holding a Senate race that could help determine control of the chamber.

“Potentially thousands of votes could be spoiled by this new guidance,” said Sailor Jones, the state director of Common Cause North Carolina. “This is a huge deal for North Carolina.”

Elections officials began mailing ballots on Sept. 4, making North Carolina the first state to do so ahead of the Nov. 3 midterms. That same day, the North Carolina State Board of Elections sent a memo to county election directors about new rules. Among them was a mandate to rule an unsealed inner envelope a “deficiency” requiring a ballot to be rejected.

The inner envelope was added to mail ballots in 2023 to comply with a voter I.D. requirement when it went into effect. Voters must put their ballot in an inner envelope and include a copy of their qualifying I.D. in a sleeve outside of it; the inner envelope then goes into a separate envelope for mailing.

In previous elections, county elections offices accepted mail ballots with unsealed inner envelopes as long as the outer envelope was sealed, said Hilary Harris Klein, senior counsel for the Southern Coalition for Social Justice’s voting rights program. That changed after last month’s memo.

The State Board of Elections flipped to a Republican majority last year.

Ms. Klein said she attended a public ballot canvassing meeting in Guilford County on Tuesday during which officials were rejecting ballots with unsealed inner envelopes.

“There doesn’t appear to be any evidence of tampering or fraud or anything,” she said. The new state board, she added, has just taken a “harsher view of what voters should have to do.”

“From my perspective, they’re just tossing ballots with no evidence of a security issue,” she said.

Gerry Cohen, a board of elections member in Wake County, the largest in the state, said that about 2.5 percent of ballots were rejected over the first three weeks of mail voting because of unsealed inner envelopes. That rate had dropped slightly to about 2 percent this past week, he said. The county has received about 8,000 ballots so far.

“It has increased the number being rejected,” he said of the new guidance. “The state argued that somebody could have — since your inner envelope was unsealed — could have somehow gone into it and changed the markings on the ballot and put it back in.” He added, “I find that far-fetched.”

The North Carolina Alliance for Retired Americans, an advocacy organization, along with other groups and two voters, sued over the new rules last month. They argued that the last-minute guidance would disenfranchise voters, especially older people or people with disabilities who are more likely to vote by mail.

The plaintiffs were represented by the Elias Law Group, whose chairman, the elections lawyer Marc Elias, founded Democracy Docket, a group aligned with the Democratic Party that tracks election cases. Democracy Docket first reported on the mail-in ballot rejection rates on Tuesday.

On Monday, Judge Thomas D. Schroeder of the Middle District of North Carolina declined to block the guidance from taking effect. The plaintiffs waited 18 days after the memo to sue, a delay the judge called “significant.” And he said blocking the guidance now would be “infeasible at this stage in the midst of voting.”

Judge Schroeder also noted that voters whose ballots had been rejected could still vote, with a new mail-in ballot, in person during the early voting period or on Election Day. But voting rights advocates also worried that voters might not find out in time either to fix their ballot or to vote in person.

In a statement on Tuesday, Sam Hayes, the executive director of the State Board of Elections, praised the ruling and said the board wanted voters to participate, adding that people “must follow the rules established to protect the integrity of our elections.”

On Wednesday, the board said its data showed “a slight increase” in rejected ballot rates — up to 3.1. percent from 2.6 percent in 2022 — and noted that ballots could be rejected “for many reasons.” It urged voters to cast their ballots as soon as possible.

Gov. Josh Stein, a Democrat, emphasized that the board’s guidance was leading to more ballot rejections.

“It’s infuriating,” he said on X on Tuesday. “North Carolinians, please make a plan to vote this year, in person if possible. And if you’re voting by mail, make sure you seal both envelopes on your ballot. Don’t let them take away your vote.”

Richard Fausset contributed reporting.

item.title: Trump Administration Asks Supreme Court to Allow Border Wall Construction
item.description:
The Trump administration on Wednesday asked the Supreme Court to allow it to move forward with construction of a border wall along hundreds of miles in the Big Bend region of southwest Texas.

A federal judge in Texas had blocked construction of the barriers, which had drawn local objections. In an emergency application to the justices, Solicitor General D. John Sauer urged the justices to intervene and allow the project to proceed.

Mr. Sauer called the lower court decision “baseless,” and asserted that halting the section of the wall at issue would leave “a 300-plus-mile gap in border defenses” and “act as a dangerous magnet for cartels and other bad actors to exploit.”

A river boat guide, a church preservation group and an environmental group, along with local landowners, sued in April to stop the administration’s plan to construct barriers across more than 500 miles along the frontier with Mexico. The plan included erecting some barriers in Big Bend National Park, and it has prompted months of protests and behind-the-scenes lobbying.

The groups argued that the Trump administration had exceeded its powers under the Constitution and that the plan posed a threat to the local environment.

A federal judge in El Paso sided with the groups on Oct. 2, finding that the government had likely exceeded its authority by waiving federal environmental laws and other measures to to speed up construction.

Judge Kathleen Cardone, who was appointed by President George W. Bush, read her two-page order from the bench and ordered the Trump administration to “comply with all applicable laws.”

Lawyers for the Trump administration then asked Judge Cardone to pause her ruling, calling it “unprecedented” and “overbroad,” while they filed an appeal to the Supreme Court.

On Tuesday, Judge Cardone responded that she would keep her block in place, prompting the Trump administration’s emergency request to the justices.

The justices did not immediately announce a briefing schedule for the case.

item.title: Oregon Teacher Credited With Protecting Child Disputes Her Own Heroism
item.description:
After a teenager went on a deadly rampage at an Oregon elementary school last week, tales of heroism quickly surfaced. A father passing by who chased the attacker and killed him. A teacher who tried to tackle the gunman.

Another teacher was said to have thrown herself on top of a student during the shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Ore. But she wants to clear the record: She said she was given too much credit for her role.

“The truth is I was shot before I had any chance to act,” the teacher, Becky Drury, said in a statement released by her family on Wednesday.

A family friend of a 7-year-old child who was injured in the attack said last week that Ms. Drury had shielded the child and saved her life when the assailant fired at both of them.

But Ms. Drury, who is still hospitalized with her wounds, said she that was not how she remembered the events.

She recalled hearing a commotion outside the special education classroom and running into the hall to find out what was going on.

“I then saw the shooter and immediately ran back into the classroom,” she said. “I turned to shut the door behind me, but the shooter was already there. Before I could do anything more, he shot me at close range and I fell to the ground.”

Ms. Drury’s left arm was nearly severed by the gunshot, and her right arm was also injured, her statement said.

“I could not get up, defend myself, or protect anyone else,” she wrote. “So, I did the only thing I could do, which was to pretend to be dead in the hope he would not shoot me again.”

The police have credited several people with preventing more deaths at Silver Rail. On Thursday, the assailant, identified as 16-year-old Griffin J. John II, a former special education student at Silver Rail, jumped a fence outside the school, shot his way in through locked doors and killed three children and one teacher. Rhoam Summer, 5, was one of the slain students; the other students, who have not yet been identified, were 8 and 11. Megan Lambert, the teacher who died, was 25.

The police are still searching for a motive. Law enforcement officials have said the pump-action shotgun used in the attack had been purchased by the gunman’s mother.

The authorities have said the attacker was stopped by a father of two students at the school who saw the attack begin as he drove by on a lunch break. The father chased him into the school and shot him with a handgun. Officials have also hailed another teacher for trying to tackle the shooter and throwing her phone at him, saying that she helped slow the attack.

Ms. Drury, an inclusion education specialist who has worked at Silver Rail for eight years, spoke to the police about her experience this week, her family’s representative said.

Precise details about what occurred in the attack have been slow to emerge. The police initially said there were seven people in the classroom. This week, they updated that to say there were nine people in the room during the shooting: five children, one of whom escaped unharmed, and four adults, including two teachers who were not injured.

Students in most of the Bend-LaPine School District returned to class Wednesday morning. But Silver Rail remains closed.

item.title: Florida Mayor Is Accused of Taking Covid Grant Funds She Helped Approve
item.description:
The mayor of Kissimmee, Fla., was arrested on Wednesday on charges of theft and fraud in connection with $50,000 in Covid-19 grant funds that she and her family received from a city program she helped create, officials said.

The mayor, Jackie Espinosa, 58, was charged with grand theft and organized scheme to defraud.

“Florida taxpayers funded that money to help small businesses recover, not to enrich the mayor who controlled it,” James Uthmeier, the state attorney general, said in a statement.

Ms. Espinosa has been the mayor of Kissimmee, a city in Central Florida with a population of more than 84,000, since November 2024. She was arrested outside her home on Wednesday morning and was being held without bond.

She was booked into the Osceola County jail on a charge of theft of property valued at between $20,000 and $100,000, a second-degree felony, records show. The arrest record also cites a felony charge of organized fraud to obtain property worth $50,000 or more.

Migdalia Perez, a lawyer for Ms. Espinosa, said in a statement that her client maintained her innocence.

“There is a fundamental difference between an alleged ethics violation and a criminal offense,” Ms. Perez said in a statement. “The state cannot transform one into the other without proving every element of a crime beyond a reasonable doubt.”

In his statement, Mr. Uthmeier said the investigation showed that after Ms. Espinosa became mayor, she created a city program called Business Boost 2.0, which was funded under the economic stimulus package signed into law by President Joseph R. Biden Jr. It was intended to provide assistance to small businesses during the Covid-19 pandemic.

The statement said Ms. Espinosa and her family members applied for $50,000 in funds for three businesses they owned. The funds were deposited into accounts linked to the Espinosa family on Nov. 7, 2025, the attorney general’s statement said.

On Dec. 5, the city attorney notified the mayor that accepting the funds “created a prohibited conflict of interest,” the statement said.

Ms. Espinosa “was advised to return the money, but she declined to do so, stated she would fight any complaint, and took no corrective action,” according to the statement.

In March, a Kissimmee resident filed an ethics complaint accusing Ms. Espinosa of violating the city’s code of ethics by creating and funding grant programs that she and her family members benefited from, among other allegations.

Mayanne Downs, a court-appointed special prosecutor, investigated the allegations and found “clear probable cause” to file articles of impeachment against Ms. Espinosa, according to a report Ms. Downs filed in July.

In August, the Kissimmee city commissioners deadlocked 2-2 on a vote to move forward with impeachment proceedings against Ms. Espinosa. In September, the Florida State Ethics Commission said it had found probable cause that Ms. Espinosa had a conflict of interest in accepting grant money for her business that was administered by her agency.

Blaise Ingoglia, the state’s chief financial officer, said at a news conference on Wednesday afternoon that the state Department of Financial Services began looking into Ms. Espinosa after investigators noticed “irregularities” while auditing local governments with respect to the Covid-19 programs. Ms. Espinosa faces up to 30 years in prison if she is found guilty, he said.

In addition to the $50,000 that Ms. Espinosa and her family received, he said that an additional $40,000 went to “tenants Espinosa’s businesses,” including a dance studio, restaurant and real estate agency.Ms. Espinosa submitted the grant applications on the day the program began accepting them, Mr. Ingoglia said.

“She was one of the first ones in line” to apply, he said, adding that she was also “part of the control mechanism that approved the applications.”

Mr. Uthmeier said at the news conference that “there is zero tolerance when it comes to public corruption.”

The case will be prosecuted in the 13th Judicial Circuit.

item.title: Trump Says He’ll Decide Who Gets Rewards From New Whistle-Blower Program
item.description:
President Trump this week announced a new $25 million whistle-blower incentive program to provide information to combat fraud. But the program has raised concerns after Mr. Trump said he would personally determine who would get the money, seeming to bypass the traditional processes around the awarding of federal funds.

“I will be the arbitrator of all of these decisions,” Mr. Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. “In other words, I’ll determine whether or not the person is deserving, and I’ll determine, and I will be very generous.”

Whistle-blowers already receive hundreds of millions of dollars annually for reporting fraud through existing legal avenues, including filing complaints under the False Claims Act and whistle-blower programs at the I.R.S., the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission. Payouts under such programs are typically determined by a commission or by a federal court, not the president.

A White House spokeswoman, Lauren Bis, said that “every day, President Trump’s task force to eliminate fraud is zeroing in on the rampant abuse of taxpayer dollars.” She added: “This administration has zero tolerance for individuals who steal from Americans.”

Mr. Trump’s first award, of $10,000, went to Nick Shirley, a conservative YouTube personality who promoted allegations of fraud among the Somali community in Minnesota. Mr. Trump and other Republicans have used those allegations to attack Democrats in the state.

Joe Spielberger, senior policy counsel for the Project on Government Oversight, said what Mr. Trump laid out was “not a serious anti-fraud or whistle-blower incentive program.”

“The administration and their allies have continuously cited combating fraud as a cover to persecute political opponents and immigrant communities,” he said. “There is no evidence that tips generated from the public will be treated similarly and consistently investigated. This only incentivizes political provocateurs to target anyone the administration deems an enemy.”

Here is a look at the whistle-blower program and Mr. Trump’s announcement.

According to the White House, the “Fraud Whistle-blower Incentive Program” will be administered by the Justice Department. It would award up to $30,000 to anyone who submits a tip that leads to a successful conviction for fraud or a significant federal enforcement action.

But Mr. Trump described the program differently. The president said he would award a “1 percent commission” to the tipster based on the value of the fraud found.

“You, let’s say, report and you find a billion dollars, we are giving a commission to that person of 1 percent — a lot of money,” Mr. Trump said. “And if it’s $10 billion, $200 billion, $400 billion, we’re giving a 1 percent commission to that person.”

Under the president’s description, a whistle-blower could receive billions of dollars personally approved by Mr. Trump.

Yes, there are several programs already awarding millions annually to whistle-blowers through systems approved by Congress.

Under the False Claims Act, for instance, whistle-blowers file civil suits confidentially alleging wrongdoing. The Justice Department evaluates the claims and decides whether to join them. If a settlement is reached in which the wrongdoer repays the federal government, the whistle-blower receives up to 30 percent of the funds. Last year, after going through the court process, whistle-blowers were awarded more than $330 million.

Likewise, in fiscal year 2025, the Securities and Exchange Commission awarded $60 million to 48 individual whistle-blowers.

In announcing that he would make determinations about the payouts, Mr. Trump raised concerns that he would use the program for political purposes.

“Generally speaking, incentivizing whistle-blowers is a good thing, but is this going to be manipulated for political purposes?” said Mark Greenblatt, a former inspector general for the Interior Department. “When you concentrate discretion for spending federal dollars into one person’s hands who can make unilateral decisions, you run into potential problems.”

David Rosenfeld, a law professor at Northern Illinois University and the former co-leader for enforcement at the S.E.C.’s New York office, said there was an extensive process within the S.E.C. for awarding whistle-blower payouts, including several layers of review.

“It’s not up to one person to do it in a discretionary manner,” he said. “I’ve never heard of a program where it’s just up to the president.”

It’s true that Mr. Trump has not been uniformly tough on fraud. He has granted clemency to more than 70 allies, donors and others convicted in fraud cases, often involved high-dollar totals.

He has shown no such leniency with regard to the fraud cases in Minnesota, where immigrants and Democratic politicians are his political targets.

The president used the announcement of the fund to attack Gov. Tim Walz of Minnesota, a Democrat, as “100 percent guilty,” and the state’s attorney general, Keith Ellison, also a Democrat, as a “total thief.” And he has portrayed the lieutenant governor of Minnesota, Peggy Flanagan, who is the Democratic nominee in a Senate race, as a “liar.”

Mr. Trump also lashed out at Representative Ilhan Omar, a Minnesota Democrat and Somali American, suggesting she could “go to jail” and calling her a “sick, very dishonest person.”

Federal data does not support the suggestion of the president and his allies that fraud occurs more prevalently under Democrats than Republicans.

item.title: A Strong Poll for Democrats, With Some Warning Signs
item.description:
A new poll from The New York Times and Siena University has ominous news for Republicans: President Trump has the lowest approval rating of any president before a midterm election since the dawn of modern polling.

Sitting at 34 percent, it’s lower than George W. Bush’s was in 2006, before Democrats flipped 31 seats in the House and five in the Senate, winning both chambers. It’s lower than his own was in 2018, when Democrats flipped 41 seats in the House. It’s considerably lower than Barack Obama’s was in 2010, before the midterm “shellacking” that netted Republicans more than 60 seats in the House and six seats in the Senate.

It is not, however, lower than views of the Democratic Party.

Democrats have a lot to be happy about in this poll, including the fact that they appear to have improved their standing among groups who powered Trump’s 2024 victory: men, young voters and Hispanic voters.

But there are several bright spots for Republicans across a map that already favors them. Let’s take a look at them.

My colleague Ruth Igielnik, a polling editor for The Times, put it this way: The only people less popular than Trump are the Democrats.

Today’s poll found that just 28 percent of voters said they were satisfied with the Democratic Party, compared with 36 percent who said the same of the Republican Party. Many of those dissatisfied with the party are, in fact, Democrats themselves — 43 percent of Democrats said they were dissatisfied with their own party.

That explains why so many Democrats running in red and purple states, like Kansas, are keeping their distance from the national party. And it hints at tensions within the party that are likely to persist well beyond Election Day.

The poll found that likely voters preferred Democratic candidates over Republicans by 11 percentage points in their congressional districts. That’s a big number, my colleague Nate Cohn writes:

In this particular poll, the Democratic lead is large enough that the party would still deliver a significant victory even if it were off by as much as the polls were in 2016 or 2020.

But when our pollsters asked voters in the 35 states that have a Senate race whether they would vote for the Democrat or the Republican, the Democrats’ lead narrowed to just five points. That could be a sign that reclaiming the Senate is still a tall order for Democrats, who are trying to flip seats in several red states while battling it out in purple states, too.

It was a surprise when, last month, a Times/Siena poll showed the Democrats had a seven-point advantage over Republicans on the question of which party voters trusted more to handle immigration. After all, immigration was one of the key issues that lifted Trump back to the White House.

The latest poll showed that immigration is re-emerging as a defining concern for voters, and that the Democrats’ advantage has shrunk to four points. Nearly 20 percent of Republicans now say the issue is their top priority — nearly twice as many as those who said so last month.

One of the questions I hear most from readers is: Why should we trust the polls this year, when they were wrong in years past?

As many of you will surely recall, polling in the 2016 and 2020 presidential elections understated Republican strength. Writing about this year’s polls, Nate Cohn doesn’t beat around the bush: “Let’s state it plainly: It is absolutely possible that the polls could be overestimating Democrats.”

But Nate says there are reasons to believe midterm polling is more reliable.

Polling did not undercount Republicans in the 2018 or 2022 midterms, he notes, in part because the disengaged voters that polling misses also tend not to vote in these elections.

And polling techniques have evolved to account for the mistakes of 2016 and 2020. Many pollsters, including The Times and Siena, now rely on new methods of contacting voters and different weighting practices.

That said, polling is by its nature an inexact science. “The only thing that’s guaranteed is that the polls won’t be exactly right,” Nate writes. “They’re just not precise enough.”

One pollster you definitely shouldn’t trust: Wedgewood Polls, which purported to have conducted surveys in several battleground states this year and acknowledged last night that its operation was largely a sham. The admission came after a polling website, FiftyPlusOne, noticed inconsistencies in Wedgewood’s data.

Wedgewood claimed that its fake polls were a social experiment to prove how easy it was to dupe the news media, though some of its activities seem to conflict with that mission — including at least three appeals it made on social media for funding or sponsorship.

Get Caught Up

Vice President JD Vance defended a contentious attack ad in the Ohio governor’s race — which features the estranged mother of the Democratic candidate, Amy Acton — and slammed Republican criticism of the spot as “whining.” Acton’s opponent, Vivek Ramaswamy, plans to spend $4 million to air the ad.

A coalition of Democrats filed a lawsuit to block the Trump administration from changing how the election is administered. In particular, the suit asks that the federal government not be allowed to order states to disqualify individual voters.

A new mail-in ballot rule in North Carolina — which requires that both inner and outer envelopes be sealed — could lead to the rejection of thousands of ballots.

Brad Lander, a Democratic House candidate in New York, was detained by the Israeli military in the West Bank, where he was part of an international delegation harvesting olives alongside Palestinian farmers.

The second debate in the Michigan Senate race between Mike Rogers, the Republican nominee, and Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee, is tonight at 7 p.m. Eastern. (Follow our live coverage.)

AIPAC, the country’s leading pro-Israel lobby, plans to give as much as $9 million to a pro-Rogers super PAC.

Tonight there’s also a debate in the Kansas Senate race, which appears increasingly competitive. I’ll be covering that one.

Number of the Day

That’s how much the family of Julio Herrera Velutini, a billionaire Venezuelan banker, agreed to pay Alina Habba, a lawyer with close ties to Trump, over a four-year span.

Herrera was looking to get a misdemeanor campaign finance violation wiped from his record. Weeks after Habba began working for the family, Trump granted Herrera a full and unconditional pardon.

Crossing the Aisle

Former Senator Joe Manchin, the longtime centrist Democrat turned independent, spent today campaigning with Senator Susan Collins. Collins, a Republican, is in a tough re-election fight against a progressive challenger, Troy Jackson. Manchin praised her as “the most independent-minded person I’ve ever met.”

At one stop, a group of protesters held signs criticizing Collins’s vote to confirm Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who went on to help overturn Roe v. Wade, and calling on her to retire. Manchin shook the demonstrators’ hands and told them that he believed Collins had to remain in the Senate. “That’s the best senator in America,” he said.

Neil Bush, a brother of former President George W. Bush, announced today that he had voted for James Talarico, the Democrat, in Texas’ Senate race.

In a Facebook post, Bush praised Talarico as a “principled, pragmatic leader,” and criticized his Republican opponent, Ken Paxton, for helping Trump’s efforts to overturn the 2020 election.

“I have been a Republican for most of my life, and I still believe deeply in many traditional Republican principles,” Bush wrote. “But character matters more than party affiliation.”

ONE LAST THING

Who is the dumpling-devouring, 37-year-old Democrat closing in on the governorship in Alaska? Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, known throughout the state as J.K.T., has been a state organizer for a presidential campaign, a mountaineer, an Eagle Scout, a cellist and an extreme runner.

He describes his childhood as “feral”: He sprinted through the woods to school; traveled by ferry and bush plane to sleep on strangers’ couches for track meets; spelunked the storm-water drainage system with friends for fun. He went to Yale, but dropped out to win a seat in the Alaska House.

As a lawmaker, he helped assemble governing coalitions that brought Republicans, Democrats and independents together to run the chamber. Now, Anna Griffin writes, his governor’s race will test whether bipartisan bridge-building is a viable platform for Democrats in red states.

Taylor Robinson contributed to this newsletter.

item.title: U.S. and Israel Draw Up Plans for Renewed Strikes on Iran After Elections
item.description:
The U.S. and Israeli militaries have developed specific plans for renewed strikes against Iran after the American midterm elections, according to U.S. officials and other people briefed on the deliberations.

As planning for a short but intensive operation progresses, the U.S. and Israeli militaries have stepped up exercises, flying planes over Iraq to practice strike maneuvers. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth met with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Israel this week to discuss new strikes, U.S. officials said.

The targets would likely include Iran’s energy infrastructure, nuclear facilities, and missile and drone arsenal. Some officials say one more big round of attacks could push Iran’s economy over the brink and force the country to make diplomatic concessions after nearly eight months of conflict.

Still, there are reasons to be skeptical that a renewed war would be any more successful than the first phase of intense U.S.-Israeli strikes between February and April. Those rounds of fighting drove up energy prices and inflation around the world, eroded security in the Middle East and severely strained the Pentagon’s supply of missile interceptors.

It is also far from certain Mr. Trump will approve fresh strikes. Repeatedly this year he has vetoed plans for a return to major combat operations, including this month when the U.S. and Israeli militaries were nearly ready to attack.

All of the officials interviewed for this story spoke on the condition of anonymity to candidly discuss military planning.

Iranian officials have promised to retaliate this time by expanding their targets beyond commercial ships and energy infrastructure in the region to data centers and underwater internet cables.

They say the fighting will neither be quick nor limited.

While the United States is assembling a massive arsenal that will be fully in place by early November, diplomatic efforts have continued, as U.S. negotiators use the potential return to war as leverage with Iran to make progress on their demands on its nuclear program and control over the Strait of Hormuz.

So far, however, Iran’s negotiators have been unwilling to make concessions on the nuclear program, insisting on deferring that issue until later in the talks.

Some U.S. planners are convinced that an intensive three-day campaign could cause enough economic damage to change the Iranian position.

But U.S. officials have frequently predicted Iran’s collapse, and other Western officials noted that Iran’s government has so far weathered the pressures on its economy.

“At this point in the war, what is clear is that the conventional military campaign waged to date, and the current punishing economic sanctions and American naval blockade, have not brought the regime back to the negotiating table in a meaningful way,” said Dana Stroul, who served as the Pentagon’s top Middle East policy official in the Biden administration.

Neither Mr. Trump nor Mr. Netanyahu “has made a compelling case for how more war would change this strategic dilemma in an increasingly unstable and conflict-ridden region,” said Ms. Stroul, who is now with the Washington Institute for Near East Policy.

Israel’s election, on Oct. 27, could complicate the plans. If Mr. Netanyahu loses, he will become a caretaker prime minister, and it will be difficult for him to launch a war, experts say.

But some analysts believe that Mr. Netanyahu could leverage the prospect of an imminent joint U.S.-Israel strike to pressure his rivals into joining a unity government to manage the war, which would extend his hold on power.

After Hamas attacked Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, Mr. Netanyahu formed a unity government that brought some opposition members into a war cabinet to help make national security decisions.

“He could use this to call for a broad emergency government, but he will face deep suspicion from his political rivals,” said Mazal Mualem, an Israeli political commentator and the author of a biography of Mr. Netanyahu.

“If Iran attacks, that’s one thing, but initiating an offensive strike would be extremely difficult for him.”

Officials say there is a small possibility that Mr. Trump could decide to begin a campaign this month, but there are many political reasons that he is likely to wait until after the U.S. election, not least his own promise early this month not to strike before the vote.

The United States will not have its full complement of military assets — including three aircraft carriers, thousands of Marines, fighter jets and Special Operations forces — in place until early November. The U.S. military prefers to conduct attacks under the cover of night, and there will be increasing hours of darkness over Iran early next month.

There are also concerns that the war could spiral into a larger conflict. On Wednesday, the U.S. State Department ordered nonemergency government employees and their families to leave Saudi Arabia, as the Iran-backed Houthi militia continues to attack sites there.

A White House official said on Wednesday the administration does not comment on military plans “that may or may not exist.” Mr. Trump, the official added, was keeping all options on the table to ensure that Iran cannot acquire nuclear weapons.

Some officials say the targeting will avoid refineries and oil infrastructure because Mr. Trump is eager to prevent even higher gas prices.

Both the U.S. and Israel militaries are drafting plans for operations against Iran’s nuclear program, according to people briefed on the work. That could include an attack on Pickaxe Mountain, a deeply buried nuclear site that Iranians call Kooh Kolang.

Mr. Trump said last week that he was considering using a 22,000-pound GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb, or MOAB, against Pickaxe. Officials say Mr. Trump is enamored with the weapon in part because of its nickname, Mother of All Bombs.

But weapons specialists say that the MOAB explodes above ground, producing a wide blast, and would not likely destroy an underground site like Pickaxe, which is composed of granite. Military officials also warn that the bomb must be delivered by a slow-flying MC-130 transport plane that would be vulnerable to Iranian antiaircraft fire.

Israel and the United States came close to striking Iran early this month, but Mr. Trump again decided at the last minute to postpone the attack, according to U.S. and Israeli defense officials familiar with the details. The decision came shortly before the operation was to begin, after both militaries had made extensive preparations and placed their air forces on the highest state of alert.

The repeated planning efforts followed by Mr. Trump’s decisions against new attacks has caused “day-to-day whiplash” among military planners, said one commander, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss operational matters, as they try to stay poised to carry out whatever military option Mr. Trump decides in the coming weeks.

In each round of the war so far, Iran’s leadership has become less conciliatory, convinced that the ultimate U.S. and Israeli goal is to topple its government.

Iran’s new supreme leader, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, remains an enigma to U.S. and Israeli intelligence officials. Some officials say he is not as powerful as his father, who was killed early in the war, and that hard-line members of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps make key decisions.

Iranian officials say they are aware of the American war planning and have been developing their own new targets and tactics.

Peiman Salehi, a political analyst in Tehran, said that if Pickaxe is attacked, part of Iran’s plans to retaliate would be to strike major oil refineries in Saudi Arabia, including Aramco, because that would immediately spike oil and energy prices.

“The war has made us understand that the best leverage for pressuring Trump is increasing oil and energy prices because it will hurt the American people,” Mr. Salehi said.

Mahdi Mohammadi, a senior adviser to Iran’s negotiator Gen. Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said on social media this week that the idea that the United States would wrap up another round of strikes on Iran within 72 hours was a “fantasy” and that Iran would determine when the war would end. He noted that Mr. Trump said in February that the war would last two weeks.

“Our attacks will be more fierce, creative and different,” Mr. Mohammadi said. “We are determined and confident and strong planning has been put in place.”

Reporting was contributed by Tyler Pager, Erika Solomon, Jonathan Swan and Adam Rasgon.

item.title: 5 Things to Know About Adam Hamilton, the Pastor Running for Senate in Kansas
item.description:
Adam Hamilton, a pastor, is hoping his moderate message and local recognition could end a nearly century-long U.S. Senate drought for Democrats in Kansas.

He is looking to defeat the Republican incumbent, Senator Roger Marshall, a former obstetrician-gynecologist who was elected in 2020. The race is close, according to polls, despite the fact that Kansas has not sent a Democrat to the Senate since 1932.

The seat has become an unexpected battleground on a midterm map that has put many Republican strongholds in play amid rising frustrations with President Trump.

Here are five things to know about Mr. Hamilton.

Mr. Hamilton is the founder and pastor of Church of the Resurrection, the largest United Methodist congregation in the country, with around 24,000 members in three states. Mr. Hamilton stepped away from the pulpit in June to campaign but has said he plans to keep working as a senior pastor if he is elected. Mr. Marshall has used Mr. Hamilton’s role in the church as an attack line, deriding him as a “megachurch C.E.O.”

Mr. Hamilton is an unusual Democrat, and his candidacy has made for a surprising — and viable — campaign in a ruby-red state. He was registered as a Republican until earlier this year and had considered running as an independent. He has found supporters among moderate Democrats and some Republicans, including two of the state’s former Republican governors. He has criticized the Iran war and pointed to Mr. Marshall and Mr. Trump as reasons that costs are on the rise in Kansas. His campaign has emphasized making health care more accessible, particularly in rural areas, partly by restoring tax credits and reversing Medicare cuts made by the Trump administration.

The competitiveness of the race has been a shock to many. The Cook Political Report updated its assessment of the race this month to a tossup from leaning Republican. Republicans running across the Midwest are grappling with increasing energy prices and the unpopular war in Iran.

Mr. Hamilton is well known in the state and has struck a moderate tone that has appealed to disillusioned supporters of Mr. Trump. Mr. Marshall, meanwhile, is close to Mr. Trump, who campaigned on the first-term senator’s behalf this week. Mr. Trump has grown unpopular in Kansas, where a majority of voters recently said they disapproved of the president, according to a Times/Siena poll.

In the first nine months of the year, Mr. Hamilton raised $13.4 million, about six times as much as Mr. Marshall raised, Federal Election Commission filings show. Mr. Hamilton reported almost $10 million in the third quarter alone, compared with roughly $800,000 for Mr. Marshall. Republicans have funneled cash into the Kansas race: As of Sunday, the G.O.P.’s main super PAC had spent or reserved more than $11.6 million to support Mr. Marshall, whose fund-raising has lagged.

At least a dozen pastors, seminarians or clergy members have run for federal office as Democrats this year, according to Religion News Service. Among them is James Talarico, a Presbyterian seminarian and Texas’ Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, who, like Mr. Hamilton, has stepped away from religious commitments to campaign. Sarah Trone Garriott, a Lutheran minister who is running for Congress in Iowa, has continued preaching several times a month. Mr. Hamilton, for his part, has described voting as “an act of Christian discipleship.”

item.title: 5 Things to Know About Senator Roger Marshall of Kansas
item.description:
Ninety-four years ago. That was the last time Kansans elected a Democrat to the Senate. This year’s race is neck and neck, according to polls, and Senator Roger Marshall, the Republican incumbent, aims to keep his party’s streak going.

But increasing displeasure with President Trump’s economic policies as well as a strong Democratic opponent have Republicans in the state scrambling to shore up Mr. Marshall.

He was elected to the Senate in 2020, after spending decades running an OB-GYN medical practice in rural central Kansas. He comfortably won that election by 11 points.

Here are five things to know about Mr. Marshall’s candidacy.

On Monday night, Mr. Trump stumped for Mr. Marshall near Wichita. The president sought to credit him with being the driving force behind a new pledge to offer $8 billion in economic aid to farmers hurt by high diesel fuel prices. Mr. Marshall also campaigned with Vice President JD Vance last month.

During Mr. Trump’s rambling speech on Monday, he invoked an antisemitic trope while defending Mr. Marshall’s aggressive approach to collecting debts as a doctor. Mr. Trump said that Mr. Marshall had been cast as “some kind of a Shylock-type guy,” referring to the Jewish moneylender in Shakespeare’s “The Merchant of Venice,” whose name has become shorthand for antisemitic representations of avarice and usury.

Mr. Marshall has had to tiptoe around his support for some of the Trump administration’s policies. He has criticized its immigration enforcement actions, which have often targeted farm workers. A Times/Siena poll last month found that 55 percent of Kansans disapprove of the way Mr. Trump is handling his job as president, and that half said they thought Mr. Marshall would support Mr. Trump too much.

As elsewhere, the economy is center stage in Kansas. Amid disruptions caused by the war in Iran, Kansas’ agricultural economy has been hit particularly hard by the rising price of diesel, which is used in equipment from combine harvesters to irrigation pumps. Fertilizer costs have skyrocketed as well.

The state’s cattle ranchers were hurt by the Trump administration’s decision earlier this year to allow a flood of cheap beef imports into the United States, which lowered prices for consumers at the expense of domestic producers.

Those challenges added to the woes of farmers and ranchers who were already contending with a drought that has reduced yields of mainstay crops like corn, soybeans and wheat.

Mr. Marshall raised $2.5 million in individual campaign contributions by early October, compared with more than $4 million for Mr. Hamilton.

Since then, millions more have poured into the race on both sides from super PACs and outside donors. Even as Republicans have sought to divert campaign cash from other states to Kansas in recent weeks, Mr. Hamilton has continued to eclipse Mr. Marshall’s fund-raising.

Mr. Marshall, either personally or through his practice, filed lawsuits against more than 700 patients with outstanding bills during his decades-long career as an obstetrician-gynecologist, according to a New York Times analysis of Kansas court records. Patients were arrested in 81 of those cases for missing court dates. The unpaid bills ranged from several thousand dollars to as little as $101, and patients were routinely charged an 18 percent annual interest rate.

Mr. Marshall responded to The Times’s investigation last month, calling it “an absolute lie” and telling Fox News that he would “never want anyone to be arrested because of money that they owe myself or the hospital.” He said the lawsuits were a result of “standard practices.”

Of the state’s four living Republican former governors, none have endorsed Mr. Marshall. Two — Bill Graves and Mike Hayden — have endorsed Mr. Hamilton, while the other two, Sam Brownback and Jeff Colyer, have stayed neutral. The current governor of Kansas, Laura Kelly, endorsed her fellow Democrat.

In his endorsement, Mr. Graves wrote that Mr. Marshall had “turned his back” on Kansas and that Mr. Hamilton knew how to “disagree without being disagreeable.” Mr. Hayden’s message was much the same, accusing Mr. Marshall of putting “party and politics ahead of the people.” Regarding the Trump administration’s economic policies, he argued that Mr. Hamilton would be more “willing to stand up and say, ‘This isn’t working.’”

item.title: Clashes Darken Rally in South Carolina as Trump Seeks to Boost Darline Graham
item.description:
More than half a dozen clashes between rallygoers and protesters interrupted President Trump at an appearance in Clemson, S.C., on Wednesday night, where he had traveled to boost the campaign of Senator Darline Graham.

It was not the first Trump rally in recent days marred by protests. But the drumbeat of outbursts, followed by angry reactions by the president and his supporters, showed the deep political divide in the country as the Nov. 3 elections draw near.

Mr. Trump is in the midst of a six-day barnstorm across some the country’s most conservative states, seeking to shore up support among his fans at a time when Republicans are increasingly pessimistic about whether they can retain control of Congress.

South Carolina is among a raft of traditionally Republican strongholds that have become battlegrounds this cycle. Polling in these places shows that Mr. Trump’s policies on tariffs and the war in Iran — and their effect on the prices of gas, diesel and groceries for everyday Americans — have threatened the party’s fortunes.

The clashes on Wednesday between protesters, who interrupted Mr. Trump with screams and expletives, and rallygoers who responded with similar aggression, underscored how much is at stake in these midterms for a deeply polarized electorate.

One after the next, security officers escorted the protesters out of the arena, while the president’s fans whooped, jeered and chanted “U.S.A.” Mr. Trump did little to de-escalate the atmosphere.

“They’re terrible people,” he said after hearing one disruption.

“Who’s that guy who threw a punch?” he asked after another, appearing to celebrate when a rallygoer physically confronted a demonstrator.

Mr. Trump had traveled to this livestock facility in the northwest corner of South Carolina to help Ms. Graham at a time when polls show her in an unexpectedly tight race against her Democratic opponent, Dr. Annie Andrews.

The South Carolina governor, Henry McMaster, appointed Ms. Graham over the summer to fill out the remainder of the term of her brother, Senator Lindsey Graham, who died in July. The president then endorsed her for a full six-year term.

His choice of Ms. Graham, who had no prior political experience, in a tough political environment for Republicans has forced the party to pour resources into defending a seat in a state Mr. Trump carried in 2024 by more than 17 points.

On Tuesday, the Cook Political Report shifted the Senate race toward Dr. Andrews for the second time in less than a month, this time from Likely Republican to Lean Republican.

The rally showed signs of helping Ms. Graham, who needs to varnish her conservative credentials in a region called the Upstate, where ultraconservative voters were known to be critical of her brother for what they viewed as his soft stance on immigration and history of compromising with Democrats.

Mr. Trump drew a full house to the facility, and the crowd whooped and hollered at his punchlines on immigration and the media with energy reminiscent of his rallies in prior cycles. He invited Ms. Graham, who had spoken earlier in the evening, to join him onstage.

“This area, and most importantly its values, are ingrained in me,” said Ms. Graham, who was raised in the Upstate. “God, family, country.”

Earlier in the night, Senator Tim Scott and Representative Russell Fry, who ran against Ms. Graham in a bitterly fought primary election, vouched for her conservative bona fides.

Mr. Trump’s extensive efforts on behalf of Ms. Graham helped her win the primary election, but not without avoiding a runoff election against Representative Ralph Norman, the vice chair of the hard-line Freedom Caucus. Counties in the Upstate broke for Mr. Norman, who has been at best a reluctant supporter of Ms. Graham’s general election candidacy.

On a podcast episode that aired on Wednesday, Mr. Norman said he would vote for Ms. Graham, but his family would not. Mr. Norman also said he would not do any events with his former opponent — a promise he appeared to keep on Wednesday, when he was nowhere to be found at Clemson.

Mr. Trump spoke for about an hour and a half. At one point, he said he was in a “good mood.” At other moments, he looked into the crowd and saw men with their middle fingers in the air, then watched as security officers escorted them from the hall.

item.title: Judge Restricts D.H.S. Field Operations Aimed at Unearthing Voter Fraud
item.description:
A federal judge in California on Wednesday blocked the Homeland Security Department from carrying out most field operations focused on uncovering voter fraud in nine states as part of a broader push to identify noncitizen voters.

The ruling came less than two weeks before the midterm elections. The Trump administration has launched a blitz of operations focused on finding evidence of noncitizen voting or tying up election processes in states where it has dubiously claimed that large numbers of noncitizens are registered to vote.

The ruling covered stops and field interviews being carried out by hundreds of Department of Homeland Security agents assigned to fan out across the country in search of instances of voter fraud, under what the administration has referred to as the “Unlawful Voter Initiative.”

In a concise 19-page ruling, Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguin wrote that the stops appeared likely to hamper voter engagement and registration by a coalition of local governments and nonprofit groups. As with other initiatives in which the Trump administration has used federal immigration data to infer the citizenship status of people on state voter rolls, she wrote there were already signs that the “target lists” the government had generated contained errors and included naturalized citizens.

The Department of Homeland Security has defended its methods, saying federal officials had used multiple data sources in addition to the public voter data they pulled to further verify the identity of registrants and eliminate false positives.

Judge Martínez-Olguin stopped short of halting field operations. But she barred agents from carrying out interviews that “involve or are likely to involve persons” who agents “know, suspect, or should reasonably know or suspect are U.S. citizens.” Given the unreliability of federal citizenship data at issue in the case, it was unclear how significantly that would hamper the department’s activities.

The interests of the entities suing, “and the public’s interest in safe elections, free from interference or intimidation,” she wrote, “far exceed defendants’ purported interest in combating unlawful voting by non-U.S. citizens.”

Internal documents introduced in the case indicated that agents were directed to focus on California, Connecticut, Georgia, Missouri, Nevada, New York, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wisconsin.

Judge Martínez-Olguin, who was appointed by President Joseph R. Biden Jr., wrote that the scope of the operations also raised concerns about voter intimidation. She noted that according to agency memos, the Homeland Security Department “surveils, covertly infiltrates and interrogates the staff of nonprofits and churches conducting voter engagement” and had targeted nearly 150 such nonprofit groupsas of July.

The government had indicated it could target naturalized citizens in instances where data suggested an individual had voted before they were naturalized.

The case arose as the Trump administration has mounted a series of legal fights with election officials across the country, aiming to show a pattern of large-scale illegal voting in U.S. elections. The efforts have been largely unsuccessful, in part because many of the state and local authorities that administer and supervise elections have refused to comply with demands for access to sensitive voter rolls.

As a result, the federal authorities have compiled their own databases, underpinned by public, commercially available information that they have compared with federal records. The process has led to mistakes in some states, in part because public voter rolls do not include unique identifiers like Social Security numbers. Federal immigration records also sometimes fail to capture changes in citizenship status.

Election authorities in Los Angeles said the Justice Department’s lists of suspected noncitizen voters were so sloppily compiled that they seemed almost “performative” in nature, with thousands of names lacking Social Security numbers and other crucial identifying information. Many of the names, they said, were paired with addresses over which Los Angeles had no jurisdiction.

A spokesman for the Los Angeles County registrar’s office said the list was initially sent on a thumb drive that was unusable because it posed a risk to sensitive voter information, and called the federal demand “a data dump.”

Judge Martínez-Olguin paused her order from taking effect until Friday evening, allowing the government time to appeal. She wrote that order would lift at the end of Election Day, on Nov. 3, “or as otherwise directed by the court.”

It is illegal for noncitizens to vote in federal elections, and decades of evidence show that instances of noncitizen voting are exceptionally rare in the United States, far beneath levels that the administration alleges. Scrutiny of claims by the administration that large numbers of noncitizens voted in states like Nevada, for example, have caused the allegations to collapse.

The Homeland Security Department’s operations aimed at finding verified cases of voter fraud comes as the Trump administration has mounted a series of escalating — and largely unsuccessful — legal fights with election officials across the country, aiming to show a pattern of large-scale illegal voting in U.S. elections.

The administration has particularly singled out states led by Democrats like California, where officials have refused to comply with demands for access to voter rolls. Last week, federal prosecutors in Los Angeles gave local election officials 48 hours to verify the citizenship or segregate the ballots of 20,000 people on a list of potential noncitizens they said had been compiled by the Homeland Security Department.

When California officials said that timeline was impossible to comply with, the Department of Justice filed suit to prevent any ballots sent to those people from being counted.

On Monday, the federal authorities announced they had released from custody 28 immigrants throughout the state who they said were suspected of registering to vote or voting in California elections before becoming naturalized citizens. All had green cards and many denied ever knowingly registering or voting. The group represented a tiny fraction — roughly one in a million — of the roughly 23 million registered voters in the state.

item.title: MAGA Bingo and Questions of Loyalty: 5 Michigan Senate Debate Takeaways
item.description:
Dr. Abdul El-Sayed and former Representative Mike Rogers do not like each other.

The two Senate candidates in Michigan have spent months trying to tear each other down. During their debate on Wednesday, Mr. Rogers questioned Dr. El-Sayed’s loyalty to the country and sought to tie him to overseas Islamist groups. Dr. El-Sayed characterized Mr. Rogers as bought and paid for by corporate donors and in thrall to President Trump.

And somehow this debate was more civil and substantive than the last time they met, two weeks ago.

Polls show a tight race in a contest that could decide control of the chamber, with Dr. El-Sayed seeking to defend the Michigan seat for Democrats and Mr. Rogers hoping to give Republicans a lift by flipping it.

Here are five takeaways from their second and final debate:

After pushing during the first debate to place Dr. El-Sayed’s Muslim faith and family history at the center of the campaign, Mr. Rogers laid off just a little. He did not mention his opponent’s mother this time around.

Instead, he sought to tie Dr. El-Sayed, an Egyptian American, to the Muslim Brotherhood, a movement founded in Egypt nearly a century ago.

“If you are going to go to the United States Senate, we need to know: Are you for America or are you for these terrorist groups overseas?” Mr. Rogers asked.

Mr. Rogers somewhat clumsily suggested that Dr. El-Sayed wanted to defund the police not only in the United States, but also in Egypt — because of an open letter he signed in 2012. The letter called on Mohamed Morsi, a member of the Muslim Brotherhood who won Egypt’s first competitive presidential election, to “purge” police officials who had been loyal to the previous autocratic government.

Mr. Morsi was removed from power a year later in a military takeover.

Dr. El-Sayed asked for extra time to deliver a fuller response and then gave a clear declaration of his loyalty to the United States.

“It’s actually really quite beneath you, Mike,” Dr. El-Sayed responded. “I am proud of America. I’m proud to be an American. I’m proud of our Constitution that guarantees all of us the right to pray as we choose to pray. And the question that you would ask, that I think is actually really quite shameful as somebody who’s actually served under that Constitution, it is shameful, shameful.”

Dr. El-Sayed’s debate strategy was clear from the start: He wanted to tether Mr. Rogers to Mr. Trump and not allow his Senate rival to create any political distance from the unpopular president.

Dr. El-Sayed made a case that Mr. Trump, and by extension Mr. Rogers, was responsible for policies that have driven up the costs of fuel, groceries and other daily needs. He invited viewers to play “MAGA bingo,” in a lighthearted attempt to head off words or phrases Mr. Rogers might use to attack him. And he noted times when Mr. Rogers dodged questions about White House policy or his connections to Mr. Trump.

“The thing about MAGA is, whenever they’re talking, they are trying to distract you,” Dr. El-Sayed said. “Just remember: When they’re distracting you, they’re also trying to pick your pocket. It’s a form of corporatized bribery.”

Mr. Rogers made a pitch to the Democratic voters who opposed Dr. El-Sayed in the party’s hard-fought Senate primary race in August.

He made an explicit appeal to voters who backed Representative Haley Stevens, a moderate Democrat, particularly Black voters and Jews. Anger among some Jewish Michiganders about Dr. El-Sayed’s left-wing opposition to Israel has for months worried Democrats who want him to win.

But Mr. Rogers’s appeal to Black voters could also be significant in the general election. Black voters make up roughly 12 percent of the Michigan electorate, while Jewish voters make up less than 2 percent. Mr. Rogers cited his work on housing in Detroit and pointed to what he described as his campaign’s success with Black voters.

“We’re doing well with African Americans in the city of Detroit, in Pontiac, in Flint,” Mr. Rogers said.

A key part of Dr. El-Sayed’s electoral strategy is to build a voting coalition that looks different from how Democrats have won in Michigan in the past.

He may do worse with moderate Democrats in the Detroit suburbs, but he is banking on improving on his party’s performance in rural areas that have swung toward Republicans during the Trump years.

On Wednesday, Dr. El-Sayed pointed to his crowds during his trip last week to Michigan’s conservative Upper Peninsula. There, he said, voters brought the same concerns about high costs as people he had met elsewhere in the state.

“We had 500 people in Iron Mountain, 600 in Escanaba, 1,300 in Marquette, all coming together around a vision for an America where it just shouldn’t be this hard,” he said.

Mr. Rogers was keen to invoke his wife, which male politicians often do to try to soften their own image.

At the beginning of the debate, Mr. Rogers said “my wife and I” had decided to run for the Senate, as if she were on the ballot with him.

Later, he seemed to imply that his wife, Kristi Rogers, who worked in Iraq as a civilian employee of the Defense Department during the Iraq war, had served in the military, as he and other members of his family did.

“I wore the uniform of the United States proudly, as my son did, my wife served, my brother served, my father served,” Mr. Rogers said.

A Rogers campaign spokeswoman, Abby Ronson, said after the debate that Ms. Rogers had “felt called to serve our great country after 9/11, and we thank her for answering the call to protect Americans.”
